1 Abstract

Language offers a testbed for cognitive models that connect uncertain perception, structured representations and goal-directed action. AILM (Active Inference Language Model) explores this connection through explicit discrete generative models implemented in pymdp. Its six linguistic levels represent letters, phonemes, words, case roles, sentence types and document position. Conditional probabilities, preferences, habits and policy precision have declared meanings and inspectable parameter sources.

AILM provides a bounded alternative to learned embedding representations for studying specified linguistic mechanisms, and a potential complement to the broader predictive capabilities of large language models. Its generative core uses no transformer, neural network or learned embedding. Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) specifies the models; pymdp executes their inference and policy updates. A connected runtime exchanges conditional messages and supports next-word policy selection. This composition does not establish a globally exact posterior, and the letter generator’s expected-free-energy rule reduces to a preference-weighted softmax over the habit. These explicit mechanisms are candidates for cognitive investigation, not evidence of human-like understanding.

On a locally frozen Georgetown University Multilayer (GUM) corpus population, the connected comparison indicates lower integrated loss than disabling the named channels while retaining the same train-fitted observation encoder. This result concerns normalized letters and token spaces; full-stream closed-vocabulary word loss remains infinite because out-of-vocabulary tokens receive zero word probability. The comparison is local evidence for a fixed composition, not external replication or unrestricted language competence.

Separate component and intervention studies show that linguistic messages can help or harm a receiver; different insertion sites constrain their attribution. The accompanying gate-audit method compares thresholds with trivial baselines, typed comparators and deliberately broken variants, and binds numerical results to recorded runs through a claims ledger. Historical gates were largely repaired after construction, and held-back findings retain their stated task and uncertainty limits. The contribution is an inspectable platform for testing linguistic inference mechanisms together with an audit method that makes their failures visible. External neural models serve as supplemental reference probes; integration with them remains a proposal.

The release repository is https://github.com/ActiveInferenceInstitute/Active_Inference_Language_Model.

2 Language and Cognition Through Explicit Active Inference

2.1 Language as inference over structured representations

Language processing presents a cognitive modeling problem: observations arrive sequentially, their interpretation is uncertain, and expectations at different linguistic scales can change what a listener or reader infers. Active inference offers a framework for relating these processes through generative models, belief updating and policy selection (K. Friston et al. 2017; Da Costa et al. 2020; Parr et al. 2022). Applications to linguistic communication and active listening already demonstrate how these ideas can organize models of speaking and listening (Friston et al. 2020, 2021). The Active Inference Language Model (AILM) asks a narrower, executable question: what can be represented, composed and tested when the linguistic states and the probabilistic roles of the parameters are explicitly declared?

The motivation is mechanistic as well as predictive. A cognitive model should make it possible to specify which expectations enter a perceptual update, which preferences enter an action choice, and what changes when a message between representations is removed. AILM supplies a bounded platform for asking those questions on corpus-derived tasks. Its cognitive vocabulary motivates the modeling choices; the measurements evaluate prediction and operational label agreement. They do not validate a model of human reading, embodied meaning or neural implementation. The distinction matters because active inference’s account of cognition includes purposive interaction with the world, not just prediction of text (Pezzulo et al. 2024).

Expectation-based psycholinguistics provides a complementary starting point. Hale (2001) and Levy (2008) relate incremental processing difficulty to the surprisal of incoming language under a probabilistic model. That tradition supplies a reason to examine predictive distributions at the point where an observation arrives, rather than only aggregate text scores. Active inference additionally distinguishes belief updating from policy selection. These are related modeling questions, but neither a good predictive score nor a free-energy formulation establishes that a particular model reproduces human processing. The proposed behavioral and physiological tests in sec. 6.4 would evaluate that bridge directly.

2.2 Explicit linguistic states and their cognitive limits

AILM builds along linguistic distinctions, then makes an explicit modeling choice about how to discretize each one. Orthography, phonology, the lexicon, syntactic case role, clause type and position in a discourse supply the vocabulary for those choices. The case role is a heuristic class derived from Universal Dependencies (UD) annotation (Marneffe et al. 2021; Nivre et al. 2020). It borrows its vocabulary from the Case-Enabled Reasoning Engine with Bayesian Representations for Unified Modeling (CEREBRUM) (Friedman 2025); it is not grammatical case in UD’s morphosyntactic sense. Case grammar’s semantic relations, morphological case and a model’s assigned functional roles must be distinguished (Fillmore 1968; Blake 2001). The resulting states are operational definitions, not an assertion that this particular inventory is uniquely licensed by linguistic theory. The object is therefore a stack of agents implemented in pymdp, a Python library for discrete-state active inference (Heins et al. 2022), whose states are enumerated in the vocabulary of the field: letters, phones, words, case roles, sentence types, document-position terciles. Each builder exposes named roles: A is an emission, B is a transition, C is a log-preference over observations, and D is a prior over initial states. That semantic declaration and the parameter source are executable conformance properties; they are not a claim that every matrix was historically specified before any estimate was inspected. Each entry arrives one of two ways. It is fixed by the design — an identity emission, a positional shift, a flat preference — or it is a smoothed relative frequency, a count of a named event over a count of its condition (sec. 4.1 names which is which at every level).

These divisions are modeling hypotheses, not a consensus architecture of language. Stratificational linguistics examines relations across linguistic levels (Lamb 1966a), while constructionist cognitive linguistics examines learned generalizations linking linguistic form and function (Goldberg 2006). AILM’s named levels and message interfaces make some such distinctions experimentally accessible, but its present states do not implement a construction grammar or an embodied account of meaning.

Different corpora support different evaluations: Brown supplies letter and word statistics (Francis and Kučera 1979); the Carnegie Mellon University Pronouncing Dictionary (CMUdict) supplies pronunciation entries (Carnegie Mellon University Speech Group, n.d.); the English Web Treebank (EWT) supplies universal part-of-speech (UPOS) and dependency annotation (Silveira et al. 2014); and the Georgetown University Multilayer (GUM) corpus supplies the text population for the connected comparison (Zeldes 2017). Corpus annotation, derived task labels and the model’s observations remain distinct. Their availability does not establish that every linguistic layer of a corpus was used or evaluated.

That declaration does not live only in a builder’s variable names. Every level is additionally written down in Generalized Notation Notation (GNN), the Active Inference Institute’s text-based specification language for generative models (Smékal and Friedman 2023): a StateSpaceBlock fixes each hidden factor and observation modality and its size, and an ActInfOntologyAnnotation names which of A, B, C, D a given array is supposed to be. A conformance checker, ailm.gnn.assert_conforms, then reads a level’s declaration and its live pymdp.Agent side by side, and ailm.spec_agent.build_agent_from_spec goes further and constructs the agent from the declaration and its registered parameter artifacts, so independently authored construction paths can be compared bit for bit. Declaring the role of every slot this way matters because pymdp’s own validator has nothing to say about it: a column-stochastic matrix is equally well-formed sitting in A or in B, so a matrix placed in the wrong slot passes every check the library runs. Mutation controls plant exactly that swap against a GNN declaration and require the conformance check to fail, which is what turns the claim into something falsifiable rather than aspirational (sec. 4.1): a matrix in the wrong slot stops being a slightly different number and becomes a named violation.

What that buys is structural transparency, and it is worth being exact about where it stops. Asking which entries produced a given prediction is answered by naming a column of B and a row of A and reading the numbers, with no recovery step in between. The probability and preference arrays have declared roles and axes; policy habits and precision are explicit settings as well. This applies to generation as well as recognition. It is not the same as saying that behavior reduces to those entries: behavior over a trajectory additionally depends on the recursion that compounds them, on preprocessing, on the coupling rule where a level receives a message, on the numerical floor, and, in generation, on the policy computation. Explicitness moves interpretability from recovering a latent feature to validating a model and its implementation. It does not remove the validation.

Nor does it follow that the model explains itself. A named matrix does not say why that state ontology was chosen over another, how its entries compound along a trajectory, what smoothing did to the rare events, or whether a label such as case role or document phase validly measures the construct it borrows its name from — sec. 6.1 takes up the last of those, and the transposed emission of sec. 4.11, which every structural check in the library accepted, is the standing demonstration that a fully named model is not thereby a self-checking one. Explicitness moves the interpretability question from recovery to validation. It does not close it. Accordingly, the conformance tests validate declared array roles and the inference checks validate specified recursions; neither establishes that a case inventory or document-position partition captures a linguistic or cognitive construct. Those require evidence beyond agreement with the labels used to define the task.

What this costs is capability, and the cost is paid at every level. Discrete state-space active inference (K. Friston et al. 2017; Da Costa et al. 2020; Parr et al. 2022), realized in pymdp (Heins et al. 2022), purchases transparency by committing to small, enumerated inventories and low-order dynamics. A phoneme inventory of 39 is a real inventory; a first-order chain over it is not a real phonology. AILM models letters, phonemes, words as factored word-and-position states, case roles, sentence types, and document-position terciles across six built levels. Throughout, a level is named three interchangeable ways — its ordinal position (Level 4), the short code used in channel and score-path notation (L4), and, where a gate applies, the Stage number that audits it (Stage 2 audits L2B) — and tbl. 3 gives the full correspondence. The letter model uses first-order Markov transitions, a restricted source of context within the tradition of statistical language prediction (Shannon 1948, 1951). This manuscript makes no claim of competitiveness with neural language models, and the comparison is not one AILM is designed to win. The claim is that a system built this way can be audited to the level of individual matrix entries, and that auditing it that way turns up defects that a benchmark number hides.

2.3 A bounded alternative and potential complement to large language models

Large language models (LLMs) based on transformers learn distributed representations that support broad text prediction and generation (Vaswani et al. 2017; Brown et al. 2020). AILM makes a different representational commitment: a state denotes a declared linguistic category, and each probability array relates named observations and states. This makes it an alternative for experiments whose question concerns a specified mechanism, such as the effect of a lexical expectation on phoneme decoding. The restriction also limits its vocabulary, dynamics and expressive capacity; an explicit inventory alone provides no general-purpose semantic representation.

The contrast concerns how model roles are established. Standard next-token training does not require individual neural parameters to correspond to specified linguistic categories. Mechanistic interpretability therefore studies features and circuits recovered from trained networks (Olah et al. 2020; Elhage et al. 2021). AILM instead offers designed semantic addressability: state labels, parameter axes and probability roles are assigned at construction and checked against the implementation. Neither approach by itself proves that people can understand the model or that its categories explain cognition (Lipton 2018; Doshi-Velez and Kim 2017). Here, “semantic” refers to declared model roles, not a demonstrated theory of meaning.

Complementarity is a research direction with existing precedents. A reading model by Donnarumma et al. (2025) combines LLM text predictions with active inference for directing eye movements toward informative text. Such a division of labor suggests that learned predictors and explicit belief-and-policy models can address different parts of a cognitive task. For AILM, coupling an external predictor to a declared observation or prior interface would require its own specification, controls and evaluation (sec. 6.4). That integration is not implemented or demonstrated here. GNN is the specification layer, pymdp is the computational core, and external LLMs appear as separately evaluated supplemental probes (sec. 13). Their performance does not establish the behavior of the AILM hierarchy.

2.4 Belief updating, action selection and the scope of each result

Three things travel together under the name active inference, and this manuscript keeps them apart. The first is Bayesian filtering under a discrete generative model — the predictive prior pushed through B, corrected by the observation through A (eq. 6). The second is the variational reading of that update, under which the same recursion minimizes a free energy functional (eq. 1). The third is expected free energy, which scores policies so that an agent can act (eq. 2).

Every comprehension-level Agent built here runs with a flat C and a single action; the generation Agent is a separate controlled variant. Nothing is therefore selected and no expected free energy is computed. The historical stage score paths differ: only L1’s headline calls live pymdp filtering, and each later level’s exact or NumPy score path, with the live-Agent check that licenses it, is inventoried in sec. 4.11 and tbl. 3. The later connected comparison in sec. 5.1 executes the GNN-built agents live under the causal schedule of sec. 4.10, with its own normalized-character estimand and explicit vocabulary coverage. For the letter level and the bounded letter-to-phone check, the live recursion is the forward algorithm of a hidden Markov model (HMM) (Rabiner 1989). That equivalence is not a concession; it is what makes the verification in sec. 4.11 possible, since an independent plain-numpy HMM can only be an oracle for a decoder that is one. sec. 7 states the correspondence in full.

The third layer is exercised by the letter-generation mechanism, both in its historical standalone experiment and in connected next-word continuation. It makes the letter transition controllable — one action per letter, so choosing an action is choosing the next symbol — and takes its preference vector from the word level, which is the only non-flat C in the system. The emitted letter is then a compromise between the corpus habit in the policy prior and the lexicon’s goal in C, selected by minimizing expected free energy (sec. 4.9). Results in this manuscript are attributable accordingly. The six levels of sec. 4.3 through sec. 4.8, and six of the seven cross-level channels of sec. 4.10 — the likelihood-reweighting channel and the prior/predictive-message channels — are historical interventions on the filtering components (sec. 7), not a claim of HMM equivalence for the complete connected schedule. The remaining channel, the lexicon into letter generation, and the generation results it produces are the part that subset does not cover.

2.5 Contributions: explicit models, conditional composition and falsifiable evaluation

The contributions below span the level stack itself, each level’s GNN declaration and the conformance check that binds it to the live agent, the gate-audit-and-claims-ledger method that binds every reported number to a recorded run, and the measured cross-level interventions between representations, followed by the separately evaluated connected runtime. Comparisons against external LLM probes (Ollama, OpenRouter) are an accessory reference frame confined to a supplement (sec. 13); no result in the body depends on them.

A connected conditional runtime, evaluated separately from its component history. The current runtime builds its agents from GNN specifications and registered artifacts, schedules inter-level messages, and compares the complete named-channel configuration with disabling those channels on a locally frozen GUM population (sec. 5.1). Both arms retain the same observation encoder. The comparison reports normalized-character predictive loss and full vocabulary coverage; its closed-vocabulary whole-word loss remains explicit even when out-of-vocabulary input makes it infinite. It tests that fixed composition on that population, not global posterior exactness, individual channel benefits, semantic comprehension, or independent replication.

A language model with explicit conditional probabilities, preferences, habits and policy precision, declared in GNN and checked against what got built. The letter level (src/ailm/levels/letter.py) and the phoneme level (src/ailm/levels/phoneme.py) are pymdp Agent instances whose sequence statistics live in the transition B and whose emissions live in A; those matrices and the filtering recursion over them define those standalone components. Every level’s matrices, factors, and slot roles are additionally declared in a GNN file under gnn/models/ and checked against the live agent by ailm.gnn.assert_conforms, so the specification and the code are two sources kept in agreement rather than one source with a description bolted on (sec. 4.1). The letter and phoneme models improve on their context-free unigram baselines; the letter-to-phone decoder is the first level in the system whose emission is not the identity — letters observed, phones inferred through a learned A. Details in sec. 4.3 and sec. 4.4. The remaining built levels each have a recorded gate outcome: words as a factored model whose posterior support induces a trie (sec. 4.5), case-role assignment (sec. 4.6), sentence type over a widened symbol stream (sec. 4.7, passing on a bar registered before the artifact existed, with no held-back replication available; the case-only arm it displaced is retained as a non-passing ablation), and document-position terciles (sec. 4.8). The builders are live agents, but the later headline scores use the exact/NumPy paths just stated. The six levels have separate state representations. In the historical stage evaluations, each is scored as a separate probabilistic component. The subsequent connected runtime coordinates them through conditional messages; it does not turn them into a six-level exact joint posterior (sec. 6.1).

A stack of six levels, seven receiver interventions, and a criterion still under test. The six levels make a stack; whether they make a hierarchy depends on what passes between them. The historical standalone decoders exchange no beliefs, whereas the connected runtime now executes the causal schedule described in sec. 4.10. Those two words are used in the narrow senses sec. 4.10 fixes, alongside composition and coupling, and the historical component results alone do not establish the strongest of the four. The 7 receiver interventions were therefore built on top of that composition, and those that have run were measured one at a time; their signs disagree. The letter predictive into the letter-to-phone decoder (L1→L2B) harms it, a corrected-threshold survivor. A lexical prefix message into that same receiver (L3→L2B) helps, also a corrected-threshold survivor. The magnitudes and uncertainty are reported in sec. 4.10. The lexicon into letter generation (L3→L1g) supplies the first non-flat preference vector in the project and carries a constraint no bigram can represent (sec. 4.9). The document-position-to-clause intervention (L6→L5; narrative in code) demonstrably moves the receiver’s joint D prior against a tercile-scrambled control, but no held-out clause score under that blended prior is reported, so it is one of the three prior-only results among the seven (sec. 4.8). The receiver’s privileged-label reference indicates low sensitivity in the retained case-only arm, without constituting a hard bound. The separate privileged punctuation-type-oracle→L3 word-prior intervention was predicted to harm and did not (it does not use an L5 posterior): aggregate perplexity and the token-direction tally both favor the message under the corrected document partition, a helpful result that falsifies the predicted harm (sec. 5.10.3). What organizes results with disagreeing signs is the novel-information criterion — a message may help when it is novel to the receiver and the receiver’s likelihood is sensitive to it. The channel results and one privileged-label sensitivity reference are the whole of its evidence base; it is labeled a working hypothesis throughout. L3→L1g, L6→L5, and the oracle→L3 intervention were measured independently, not as a connected cascade.

Action selection with an explicit account of what drives it. In the letter generator, deterministic controllable transitions make the policy-conditioned state predictive a point mass, so the information-gain term vanishes. The identity emission then indexes preferences by the emitted symbol, yielding \(\sigma(\gamma \mathbf{C} + \ln \mathbf{E})\): preference and corpus habit jointly determine selection (eq. 17, sec. 4.9). The derivation and contrasting stochastic-transition, flat-likelihood and action-independent controls identify which assumptions cause the reduction. A separate budgeted-attention experiment exercises information seeking in letter-to-phone decoding, but loses to an exhaustively optimal fixed observation schedule (sec. 6.1). These results distinguish implemented policy mechanisms from a generic appeal to active inference; they do not demonstrate an advantage for adaptive attention or embodied agency.

Mis-specified gates, diagnosed and re-derived. The original Stage 1–4 gates were repaired after their levels had already been built or measured, and later stage declarations were re-scoped during audit. Two early gates fail in opposite directions and are worked through here. The Stage 1 gate demanded a gain over uniform larger than the first-order information the training distribution contains. The Stage 2 gate demanded an accuracy that a context-free lookup table already exceeds, and specified it against a treebank with no phonemic annotation. One gate was out of reach of its own model class, the other free, and both were accepted without a baseline or a comparator having been measured. scripts/audit_gates.py reports every stage as VACUOUS, UNREACHABLE, ABOVE_REFERENCE, BRACKETED_BOUND, BRACKETED_REFERENCE, or UNAUDITED from its measured trivial baseline and its typed comparator, so the check is an artifact rather than an act of attention. sec. 4.2 develops the classification, states which population each baseline and ceiling was measured on, and tabulates every stage’s verdict.

A comparator stronger than the model it was meant to floor. The gate audit’s sharpest single finding is mechanistic rather than procedural: a left-context lookup table, fitted on training data alone with no latent state and no inference at decode time, outperforms the shipped letter-to-phone filter, so clearing the weaker context-free bar did not show the latent-state machinery doing the work (sec. 10.1.6).

Verification apparatus, treated as a result. pymdp validates that matrices are normalized, which is not the same as validating that they are in the right slot — a bigram matrix is column-stochastic whether it sits in A or in B. AILM therefore verifies numerically rather than structurally, and the apparatus is sized to the claim surface it defends. A closed-form HMM oracle in plain numpy (src/ailm/verification/oracle.py), forbidden by test from importing pymdp, decodes identically to the shipped decoder across a bounded equivalence subset; full-set attribution to pymdp is an extrapolation from those checked positions (sec. 6.1). A control harness (src/ailm/control.py) requires a positive and a negative control per gate and raises GateVacuousError when they fail to separate. Multiplicity accounting reports which members of the declared significance family survive fixed Bonferroni and Holm step-down correction (sec. 15.2). A claims ledger (src/ailm/claims.py) binds every quantitative statement in this manuscript to a recorded run. None of these instruments was designed in advance. sec. 4.11 pairs each with the shipped defect that motivated it.

2.6 Testing linguistic mechanisms with baselines and broken controls

AILM’s prospective method prescribes building one level at a time and opening a level only after the one below it has passed a falsifiable gate. The historical build did not consistently follow that prescription, as the chronology below states. Three requirements on the gate itself are:

  1. Use an informative trivial baseline. For a claim that a letter or phone model uses context, marginal symbol frequencies provide the appropriate context-free baseline. Beating uniform alone can reflect only frequency knowledge. Other claims need their own named baseline: a word model is compared with a letter bigram, and a clause mixture with a type-free chain. The baseline must remove the mechanism the gate purports to test.
  2. The gate must be bracketed before it is accepted. Measure what the trivial baseline scores and what the model order can achieve. If the baseline already satisfies the threshold, the gate is vacuous; if the ceiling cannot reach it, the gate is unreachable. A threshold strictly between those scores separates those comparators; it still needs mechanism-specific controls.
  3. The gate needs a relevant negative control that actually fails. A deliberately broken variant is run against the same threshold and must not pass. Stage 1’s mis-wired agent and Stage 2’s transposed-transition and corrupted-emission controls are kept in the test suite for exactly this purpose.

The third requirement is what makes the first two enforceable, and the second is exactly where the Stage 1 and Stage 2 gates above failed: neither had its ceiling or its baseline measured before it was accepted.

2.7 Reading the evidence: development findings and held-back tests

Numbered decisions cited throughout are entries in the repository’s chronological decisions log, docs/decisions.md, released with the code; each records a design choice or a measured outcome, including every null. Quantitative statements in this manuscript use the following strength labels, and the prose holds each result to its label. Corrected-threshold survivor: the effect crosses the fixed Bonferroni per-test threshold for the declared family of 16 significance tests at \(\alpha =\) 0.01; 7 tests do, including the helpful lexical channel and the harmful coupling channel. Step-down survivor: the effect crosses its Holm threshold at the same familywise level and under the same dependence assumptions, but not the fixed one; none does (sec. 15.2). Nominally significant: the test whose prediction was timestamped before its measurement crosses the uncorrected familywise level but neither corrected threshold. None of these three labels means confirmed. Each names a threshold crossed on a population that had already contributed to building the family — each is a retrospective-family threshold survivor on the reused development population — and a familywise correction bounds a fixed family’s Type-I rate rather than restoring independence to a reused split (sec. 15.2). Non-passing, unresolved: the shipped comparison does not clear its bar and the paired gain interval spans zero. It is reported with uncertainty on every intervalled axis and with a control showing that the same machinery recovers a deliberately larger planted effect; that control does not prove power for the real effect at the shipped operating point. The retained case-only clause ablation (sec. 4.7) holds this status. Passing on a development-session specification: the bar was registered before the artifact that answers it existed, so it could have failed and did not, but registration and outcome share one session and no held-back partition remains on which to replicate it. It licenses less than a confirmatory result and more than a restated bar, and it is reported with both halves of that sentence every time. The canonical clause level (sec. 5.7.3) holds this status. Working hypothesis: the claim organizes the design but is bounded by the evidence that produced it; the novel-information criterion for cross-level channels (decisions 18–19) is stated over the measured channels and the privileged-label receiver-sensitivity reference that supports it, never as a universal rule. These labels delimit the intended interpretation; they do not replace checking the population, comparator and uncertainty. The claims ledger (sec. 4.11) makes every label auditable against a recorded run.

A qualification governs every label and belongs here rather than in the limitations. The original Stage 1–4 gates were restated after their levels were built or measured because the thresholds were vacuous, unreachable, or named the wrong population; later stage declarations were re-scoped during audit (tbl. 22). Stage 6’s directional prediction was committed before its held-out measurement, but the development population and analysis family were reused, and the document-clustered primary analysis is non-confirmatory. The method therefore includes retroactive re-certification and does not establish a prospective sequential build. Converting any label into ordinary confirmation requires a frozen rerun on a population untouched by development. That rerun was pre-registered, executed to its first data touch, and retired by exhaustion for the external_lexicon members (decision 91); the ud_ewt_test members were then scored exactly once against the held-back EWT test split under decision 111 (sec. 10.6): two clear the frozen per-test bar in their recorded direction, two yield no discordant pair, and the other twelve members of the family remain development-population inference.

2.8 Relation to prior language models in active inference

Active inference has reached language before: Friston et al. (2020) simulate generation and comprehension in a deep discrete model on a constructed Twenty Questions task; the narrower contribution here is to fit such models to natural corpora and score them on held-out text. To our knowledge, following searches of arXiv, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar through August 2026 whose full record is published with this work, no earlier system satisfies the joint corpus-fit and held-out-metric criterion; the broader index searches were incomplete (rate-limited), so this is a bounded no-counterexample report and the manuscript makes no priority claim.

2.9 Organization of the manuscript

sec. 3 fixes notation: variational and expected free energy, the discrete generative model, the filtering recursion, perplexity, and the empirical conditional-entropy optimum, followed by the CEREBRUM case inventory (Friedman 2025, 2026) that the built Level 4 uses (sec. 4.6). sec. 4.1 gives the level stack and states the rule that sequence dynamics belong in B, and sec. 4.2 formalizes threshold placement. sec. 4.3 through sec. 4.8 report the six built levels; sec. 4.9 reports generation by policy selection and sec. 4.10 the measured cross-level channels. sec. 4.11 covers the oracle, the control harness, and the claims ledger; sec. 5 collects the measurements; sec. 6.1 states what the length-matched subset, the order-1 dynamics, and the historical standalone decoders and the conditional connected schedule rule out; sec. 7 positions the work; and sec. 8 gives the commands. The supplements follow the conclusion: sec. 10 carries the gate-audit trails and the confirmatory replication, sec. 11 the channel factorial, sec. 12 reports complexity, sec. 13 scores the registered zero-shot external models and an AILM comparator on letter, phoneme, and position-aligned letter-to-phone next-symbol tasks, sec. 14 presents the machine-checked Lean layer, and sec. 15 supplies statistical details. The external benchmark uses identical units and a bounded response contract, but its prose fixture and phoneme comparator are its own rather than the body’s. It is therefore a reference frame rather than a competitiveness claim, and no result in the body depends on it. sec. 6.4 gathers the next steps this record opens rather than closes — including where an explicit system built this way and a learned one might call each other — as proposals to be built and measured, never as results reported here.

3 Generative Models of Linguistic Belief and Action

Every matrix named in this section appears under the same name in the source: A, B, C, and D are the arguments to the pymdp Agent constructor in every level module under src/ailm/levels/. tbl. 1 is the symbol registry: each symbol in it has exactly one meaning, fixed by an equation below. The registry covers the formalism, not every letter in the paper. Among the symbols outside it, \(\alpha\) and \(P\) have context-dependent meanings. \(\alpha\) is a channel mixing weight in the sweeps, a significance level in the multiplicity accounting, and, subscripted, the forward-algorithm message \(\alpha_t\) (sec. 4.11) and the case level’s likelihood weight \(\alpha_c\). \(P\) is a probability wherever it takes an argument, as in the clause level’s type prior \(P(\text{type})\) (sec. 4.7); it is the evaluation population indexing a gate verdict in eq. 12, where the baseline and ceiling measured on that population are written \(b_P\) and \(c_P\); and it is the size of the word level’s position factor in the memory accounting of sec. 12. Each use is fixed by its subscript, its argument, or the sentence that introduces it; no registry symbol is reused.

Table 1: Symbol registry for the formalism. Each registered symbol has exactly one meaning throughout the paper; the predictive prior is \(\rho_t\), not \(\pi\), precisely so that \(\pi\) can mean policy unambiguously. Symbols outside this table are not covered by that guarantee — \(\alpha\) and \(P\) in particular are reused, and the text above says where.
Symbol Meaning Defined in
\(\pi\) policy (sequence of actions) eq. 2, eq. 3
\(\rho_t\) one-step predictive prior over states eq. 6
\(q_t\) filtered posterior after observing \(o_t\) eq. 6
\(\tilde{q}\) policy-conditioned predictive over \((o_\tau, s_\tau)\) eq. 2
\(\tilde{p}\) preference distribution, \(\mathbf{C}_i = \log\tilde{p}(o=i)\) eq. 5
\(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D}\) the likelihood, transition, preference, and prior matrices; \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are column-stochastic in the conditioning index eq. 5
\(\mathbf{E}\) prior over policies, the agent’s habit: what it would do under no preference and no informative epistemic value at all sec. 4.9

3.1 Perceptual belief updating and variational free energy

An active inference agent holds a generative model \(p(o, s)\) over observations \(o\) and hidden states \(s\), and an approximate posterior \(q(s)\). Perception minimizes variational free energy, which decomposes into a complexity term and an accuracy term and bounds the negative log evidence (Friston 2010; Parr et al. 2022; Smith et al. 2022). The complexity term uses Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence:

\[F[q] \;=\; \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[\, q(s) \,\big\|\, p(s) \,\right]}_{\text{complexity}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(s)}\!\left[\log p(o \mid s)\right]}_{\text{accuracy}} \;\geq\; -\log p(o) .\qquad{(1)}\]

When the family over which \(q\) ranges contains the exact posterior, minimizing eq. 1 returns it, and the update is closed-form rather than iterative. The isolated filtering components meet that condition under their stated observations and priors, though not all in the same way. Levels 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 carry a single hidden factor, so an unrestricted categorical \(q\) trivially contains the posterior. Level 3 is genuinely two-factor and meets the condition for a different reason: its position factor is degenerate at every step — \(\mathbf{D}[1]\) is a point mass and \(\mathbf{B}[1]\) the deterministic shift (sec. 4.5) — so the exact joint posterior is already a product and lies inside the factorized family. This exactness claim concerns each declared conditional update. It does not establish a globally exact posterior for the connected message schedule. The exactness is a property of those conditional updates, not of mean-field active inference in general, where a restricted \(q\) need not contain the posterior and minimizing eq. 1 returns the closest member of the family instead.

3.2 Action selection: information seeking and preferred outcomes

Action selection minimizes expected free energy (EFE), \(G(\pi)\), over policies \(\pi\). Under the standard decomposition it splits into an epistemic term rewarding information gain about hidden states and a pragmatic term rewarding observations the agent prefers (Friston et al. 2015; Da Costa et al. 2020; Parr et al. 2022):

\[G(\pi) \;=\; -\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{q}}\!\left[\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[\, q(s_\tau \mid o_\tau, \pi) \,\big\|\, q(s_\tau \mid \pi) \,\right]\right]}_{\text{epistemic value}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{q}}\!\left[\log \tilde{p}(o_\tau)\right]}_{\text{pragmatic value}} ,\qquad{(2)}\]

where \(\tilde{p}(o_\tau)\) is the preferred-observation distribution encoded by the log-preference vector \(\mathbf{C}\), and \(\tilde{q}(o_\tau, s_\tau \mid \pi) = p(o_\tau \mid s_\tau)\, q(s_\tau \mid \pi)\) is the policy-conditioned predictive over outcomes and states, the measure under which both expectations in eq. 2 are taken. AILM’s generation mechanism is policy selection under eq. 2 with \(\mathbf{C}\) supplied top-down by the level above; the decoding paths do not exercise it, because during comprehension each level has a single trivial action and \(\mathbf{C}\) is zero. Generation is built and measured in sec. 4.9, and the document-position (tercile) level, narrative in code, reaches the clause level only through a blended D prior, not through policy selection (sec. 4.8).

Policies are scored by \(G(\pi)\), but they are selected against a prior over policies as well, \(\mathbf{E}\) — informally the agent’s habit: what it would do under no preference and no informative epistemic value at all. The two combine as a softmax over expected free energy shifted by a log-habit term (K. Friston et al. 2017; Da Costa et al. 2020), so that where \(G(\pi)\) carries no information — a flat \(\mathbf{C}\) and an epistemic term that vanishes — the policy posterior collapses onto the habit alone. AILM’s one generative level exercises exactly that combination, and sec. 4.9 gives the closed form it reduces to there.

3.3 Representing linguistic states with explicit probability arrays

AILM’s levels are discrete partially observable Markov processes, in the sense formalized by K. Friston et al. (2017) and Da Costa et al. (2020). Observations are conditionally independent given the current state, and states evolve as a first-order Markov chain under the selected policy:

\[p(o_{1:T}, s_{1:T}, \pi) \;=\; p(\pi)\, p(s_1) \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(o_t \mid s_t) \prod_{t=2}^{T} p(s_t \mid s_{t-1}, \pi) .\qquad{(3)}\]

Definition 1 (The AILM matrix tuple). A level of AILM is the tuple \(\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D} \rangle\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) and every action slice \(\mathbf{B}^{(u)}\) are column-stochastic: their columns, indexed by the conditioning variable, sum to one.

The entries of the tuple are defined in eq. 4:

\[\mathbf{A}_{ij} = p(o = i \mid s = j), \quad \mathbf{B}^{(u)}_{ij} = p(s_{t+1} = i \mid s_t = j,\, u), \quad \mathbf{C}_i = \log \tilde{p}(o = i), \quad \mathbf{D}_j = p(s_1 = j),\qquad{(4)}\]

\[\mathcal{M} \;=\; \langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D} \rangle\qquad{(5)}\]

pymdp checks normalization, dependency dimensions and indices, control-factor consistency, and restrictions imposed by the selected inference algorithm. Those structural checks still cannot infer a compatible matrix’s semantic role: the same square learned matrix can satisfy the relevant shape and normalization contracts in either the \(\mathbf{A}\) or the \(\mathbf{B}\) slot, but placing it as an emission rather than a transition expresses a different model (sec. 4.1).

The factored word and joint clause levels generalize eq. 3 without leaving it. Level 3 factorizes the hidden state into word identity and within-word position, with a single letter modality depending on both factors, so the definition applies factor-wise and each factor carries its own transition slice (sec. 4.5). Level 5 runs the construction in the other direction, embedding a two-component mixture of widened-symbol chains (case role, VERB, AUX) as one factor over a joint type-by-symbol state space with a block-diagonal transition (sec. 4.7). Level 5 is the single-factor object in different coordinates; Level 3 is not, and stays exact for the degeneracy reason given above rather than by reducing to one factor. eq. 6 and eq. 7 below are stated for one factor and applied to the factored levels through their joint state space. Nothing in this section assumes more structure than eq. 3 declares.

3.4 Sequential inference: expectations corrected by observations

Every built level consumes one symbol at a time. Given the posterior \(q_{t-1}\) over the previous state, the predictive prior \(\rho_t\) is pushed through \(\mathbf{B}\) and then corrected by the observation through \(\mathbf{A}\) (Da Costa et al. 2020), the same predict-then-correct recursion given as the forward algorithm for a hidden Markov model by (Rabiner 1989):

\[\rho_t(j) \;=\; \sum_k \mathbf{B}_{jk}\, q_{t-1}(k), \qquad q_t(j) \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{A}_{o_t j}\, \rho_t(j)}{\sum_k \mathbf{A}_{o_t k}\, \rho_t(k)} .\qquad{(6)}\]

In pymdp the two halves of eq. 6 are update_empirical_prior and infer_states respectively. Filtering conditions only on observations up to \(t\); it never revisits them. That is a modeling commitment rather than a convenience: the L3→L2B lexical channel consumes exactly such a streaming quantity — the L3→L2B message is conditioned on the letter prefix rather than the whole word (sec. 4.10). Filtering also costs accuracy relative to whole-sequence smoothing; sec. 4.4 quantifies that cost.

3.5 Predictive evaluation and the limits of first-order context

The predictive probability of the observation at step \(t\) is the denominator of eq. 6, so the per-symbol perplexity of a sequence follows directly from its cross-entropy (Shannon 1948), in the language-model convention of (Jelinek 1997; Brown et al. 1992):

\[\mathrm{PPL} \;=\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \sum_j \mathbf{A}_{o_t j}\, \rho_t(j)\right) .\qquad{(7)}\]

The relevant reference for a first-order model is not zero entropy. It is the conditional entropy of the training distribution — the smallest expected log loss any first-order conditional achieves on that distribution:

\[H_{\text{train}}(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) \;=\; -\sum_{i,j} p_{\text{train}}(i, j) \log p_{\text{train}}(i \mid j), \qquad \mathrm{PPL}_{\min} \;=\; \exp H_{\text{train}}(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) .\qquad{(8)}\]

The name matters as much as the subscript. This quantity is the empirical first-order optimum on a specific finite sample, not a distribution-free lower bound. Calling it a floor requires specifying the distribution on which it is an optimum; an evaluation-sample reference and a training-sample reference are different quantities.

The subscript on \(H_{\text{train}}\) states exactly what eq. 8 licenses and what it does not. It is the optimum of the order-1 model class on the empirical training distribution: the empirical conditional \(p_{\text{train}}(i \mid j)\) minimizes expected log loss among all first-order conditionals when the expectation is taken under \(p_{\text{train}}\), so no order-1 model scores below it there. It is not a lower bound on held-out cross-entropy. The held-out sample is a different empirical distribution whose own first-order optimum can sit on either side of this one: a held-out passage can be more or less predictable than the corpus a model was fitted to. A held-out score below \(\mathrm{PPL}_{\min}\) is therefore unexpected rather than impossible, and no claim in this paper rests on ruling it out.

What the quantity supports instead is a statement about a declared threshold, which is what sec. 4.2 needs from it. Measuring eq. 8 costs one pass over the bigram counts and answers a question that no run can answer: how much first-order information the training distribution contains at all. The Stage 1 target of 2 nats of gain over uniform demands more than that entire first-order budget by a factor of 1.95, so the bar was calibrated for a model class the level does not implement — a miscalibration finding about the threshold, not a theorem about the evaluation population. sec. 4.2 turns that into the verdict UNREACHABLE, which eq. 12 licenses only against a comparator typed as a bound — for Stage 1 the audited ceiling is the evaluation passage’s own order-1 optimum (eq. 21), measured on the same held-out prose as the model, while the training-distribution quantity above is the miscalibration diagnostic; the two populations are named wherever the comparison is made.

3.6 Linguistic case and cognitive roles: the CEREBRUM hypothesis

Level 4 of the stack assigns a case-role label — a heuristic syntactic role class derived from UD annotations, not grammatical case (sec. 4.6) — following the CEREBRUM formalism (Friedman 2025) and its categorical companion (Friedman 2026). CEREBRUM is this author’s own framework, so it is a hypothesis source for this paper and not independent validation of it. Where the prose says CEREBRUM defines or predicts something, that is a statement about an engineered ontology with an archival record. Where it says a case distinction is established, the support is the linguistic literature the case system comes from (Fillmore 1968; Blake 2001), which is independent of both this paper and CEREBRUM. Level 4’s gate is scored against Universal Dependencies annotation (sec. 4.6), also independent of both. CEREBRUM applies its case vocabulary to noun phrases, where a case is the grammatical relation a phrase bears to its predicate, and to models, where a case is the functional role a model plays among interacting agents.

The archival identity itself has a version conflict that this paper preserves rather than normalizes away. The exact Zenodo record calls the deposited work v1.4 and dates it 2025-04-16; the title page of that deposited Portable Document Format (PDF) file prints v1.2 and 2025-04-12. data/reference_sources.json records both identities, the exact filename and digest, and every PDF locator used below.

AILM keeps linguistic labels and model-function labels as distinct enumerations in src/ailm/cases.py; tbl. 2 lists them as separate inventories, not rowwise equivalents. The source’s core Genitive model role is retained as CORE_GENITIVE. A different novel Generative role appears in Supplement 2.12. CEREBRUM labels both [GEN]; AILM therefore uses CORE_GENITIVE and NOVEL_GENERATIVE with scoped serialized values while preserving the shared source abbreviation as provenance.

CEREBRUM Supplement 11 does not give every case a pair of scalar weights. It gives a likelihood weight only to Nominative and a complexity weight only to Accusative. Genitive, Dative, Instrumental, Locative, Ablative, and Vocative instead augment the latent state with, respectively, relationship, goal, action, environment, origin, and communication variables, then state case-specific precision relations. CEREBRUM_CASE_FORMULATIONS preserves those distinctions. case_conditioned_free_energy is deliberately narrower: it implements only the scalar Nominative/Accusative approximation and fails closed for every augmented-latent case. Its numerical weights in AILM_SCALAR_CASE_WEIGHTS are project-owned defaults satisfying the source inequalities, not values reported by CEREBRUM.

Unlike eq. 2, which sec. 4.9 exercises, this scalar scaffold is called by nothing outside its unit tests. Level 4 is built (sec. 4.6) but does not evaluate it — the level’s gate rests on case agreement, not on a free-energy quantity, and wiring the scaffold in without a falsifiable measurement would be decoration.

\[F_{\text{AILM-scalar}}[q;c] \;=\; \beta_c \, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[\, q(s) \,\big\|\, p(s) \,\right] \;-\; \alpha_c \, \mathbb{E}_{q(s)}\!\left[\log p(o \mid s)\right], \qquad c \in \{\mathrm{NOM},\mathrm{ACC}\} .\qquad{(9)}\]

Comparing eq. 9 with eq. 1 locates the implemented approximation exactly: Nominative reweights the likelihood term and Accusative reweights the complexity term. The equation is not asserted for the other core cases.

Cautions carry forward. CEREBRUM Supplement 8.1 defines the tuple \(\langle S, A, T, \Omega, O, F, \pi \rangle\): notably, its \(A\) is an action space, \(O\) is the likelihood, \(F\) is variational free energy, and \(\pi\) denotes precision parameters. Figure 13 is only a caption in the deposited PDF and does not supply a crosswalk. AILM_PYMDP_HEURISTIC_CROSSWALK is therefore an explicit project heuristic: source \(T\) corresponds structurally to pymdp B and source \(O\) to pymdp A, while pymdp C, D, and E have no direct source tuple analogue. In particular, source \(\pi\) is not pymdp E, and source \(F\) is not pymdp G. The decision and alternatives are recorded in docs/design/cerebrum_mapping.md. And the case oracle built from Universal Dependencies deprel labels is a research claim, not ground truth: English marks only Nominative, Accusative, and Genitive morphologically, so UD_DEPREL_TO_CASE derives the remaining roles from syntactic annotation. Agreement with that oracle is agreement, not accuracy, and sec. 10.1 treats the Stage 4 gate description accordingly — the original threshold was vacuous on gold morphology and above every measured, exceedable comparator on the derived oracle. Decision 16 records the historical UNREACHABLE wording; decision 75 corrects it to ABOVE_REFERENCE.

4 Model Construction, Conditional Coupling, and Falsifiable Verification

This section specifies the components and their connected execution. It states the level architecture, each level’s GNN declaration and the conformance check that binds it to the live agent, the gate-audit taxonomy every threshold in this paper is classified by, the construction of each of the six modeled levels and the generation path, the cross-level interventions and the hypothesis they test, and the verification apparatus that binds every reported number to a recorded run. Outcomes are reported in sec. 5.

4.1 Implemented levels and interface boundaries

sec. 3 fixed the notation; this section assigns it to the levels the rest of the paper measures. It names the stack, states the rule that keeps sequence dynamics in the transition matrix, and distinguishes historical standalone score paths from the connected conditional schedule in sec. 4.10.

4.1.1 Named factors and matrix slots

AILM is a stack of pymdp agents, one per linguistic level from letters up to document-position terciles. Each level owns its own \(\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D} \rangle\) from eq. 5, each level’s state space is enumerable and named, and no matrix is shared between levels. 6 levels are built this way; the speech row of tbl. 3 is an interface contract rather than an agent, and is marked as one wherever it appears. fig. 1 shows the stack together with the emission of each level, which is the fastest way to see where the learned statistics sit.

The case-level observation is a universal part-of-speech (UPOS) tag from UD annotation (Marneffe et al. 2021). The speech interface handles ARPAbet phonetic symbols; digital signal processing (DSP) is outside the model stack.

Table 3: The AILM level stack as implemented. Earlier drafts of the design merged clause and case into one level; the shipped stack splits them — case is L4, clause structure is L5 above it — and the speech row is deliberately an interface, not a model: DSP sits outside the level stack (docs/design/speech_boundary.md).

Every modeled row has a live pymdp.Agent builder. tbl. 4 separately states whether the recorded headline score calls that Agent’s application programming interface (API) for inference; a builder and conforming matrices do not turn an exact or NumPy scorer into live pymdp inference.

Reading each hidden factor alongside its observation shows what each level is for. At Levels 1 and 2A the emission is the identity, so the observation is the state and the level’s content is entirely its next-symbol prediction. At Level 2B and above, the observation and the hidden variable are drawn from different alphabets and the posterior is an inference: the co-indexed phone from a letter (sec. 4.4), word identity from a letter prefix (sec. 4.5), case roles from tags (sec. 4.6), sentence type from a case-role prefix (sec. 4.7), document-position tercile from sentence types (sec. 4.8). Those are latent-variable semantics, not a claim that every recorded score was produced by Agent.infer_states.

4.1.2 Declared and measured parameter counts

Every entry of every matrix in tbl. 3 arrives one of two ways. A declared entry is fixed by the design and is the same number whatever corpus is read: the identity emissions at Levels 1 and 2A, the word level’s spelling table and its two structural transitions, the clause level’s symbol read-off and the zero mass it places on every cross-type transition, the flat \(\mathbf{C}\) every level carries while it is comprehending rather than generating. A counted entry is a smoothed relative frequency estimated on a training split — a count of a named event over a count of its condition — installed as a fixed array before inference begins.

Each level therefore has one place where its corpus knowledge lives, and it is worth naming per level because it moves. Levels 1 and 2A keep it in the transition, as the Brown letter bigram and the CMUdict phone bigram, with the phone level’s start prior counted as well. Level 2B keeps it in both slots at once: a letter-given-phone emission and a phone bigram, both estimated on the training half of the split. Level 3 keeps it in the prior. Its emission is deterministic and both of its transitions are structural constants, so the lexicon with its frequencies is the level’s entire learned content, and a wrong \(\mathbf{D}\) there is what a wrong \(\mathbf{B}\) is elsewhere (sec. 4.5). Level 4 counts all three of emission, transition and start distribution. Level 5 counts its transition and its start over the joint type-by-symbol space while its emission stays deterministic, and Level 6 counts its type-given-phase emission and its phase transition, whose left-to-right support is structural even though its entries are counts. sec. 4.11 reports the one place a matrix is estimated inside pymdp instead of counted outside it, and that the two procedures are the same arithmetic.

4.1.3 Cross-level channels and shared alphabets

Hierarchical here names a relation between representations. Each level’s hidden state space is a different description of the same text, running from the symbol to the document — letters, phones, words, case roles, sentence types, document-position terciles — and the upper level’s observation alphabet is the lower level’s hidden state space where letters enter the letter-to-phone model and sentence types enter the narrative level. The word, case and clause seams are looser, and saying so costs nothing. The word level reads letters over a within-word alphabet of its own, the lowercase letters plus an end-of-word symbol, and the historical case-level evaluation reads UPOS tags from treebank annotation. The connected raw-text mode instead derives a soft UPOS observation through a train-fitted lexical encoder, whose boundary is stated in sec. 4.10. The clause seam was an identity while the clause level observed case roles alone. The canonical clause level observes the case roles plus VERB and AUX, so its alphabet strictly contains Level 4’s hidden state space rather than equaling it, and material Level 4 does not represent enters the level above it. That containment is not a detail of bookkeeping: it is the open stratificational question sec. 6.2 states and does not resolve, and it is why the retained case-only ablation, whose seam is a true identity, is kept rather than discarded.

That relation is representational, and it is what the shipped stack is. Whether the stack also earns the word in the stronger sense — a level above making the level below better — is a separate and measurable question, and it is the one sec. 4.10 answers channel by channel. One thing the representational relation does not carry is worth fixing here: it does not make the levels stages of one pass over one index. In the historical component experiments, each runs or is scored on its own index against its own artifact, and fig. 5 draws the displayed inference paths each on its own index for exactly that reason.

In these historical standalone constructions, levels compose through their alphabets rather than through an active channel. The connected schedule of sec. 4.10 adds explicit messages to those component models. Level 2’s letter-to-phone model observes the 30-symbol letter alphabet that is Level 1’s hidden state space, and infers over the 39-phone inventory, so its emission \(\mathbf{A}_{lp} = p(\text{letter } l \mid \text{phone } p)\) is a rectangular matrix linking two different alphabets of two different sizes. It relates a letter to the phone that shares its index in an equal-length word, which is a stipulated pairing rather than a recovered grapheme-to-phoneme alignment (sec. 4.4). That alphabet identity is fixed when the matrices are built and is not a value computed at run time: two agents indexing the same symbol set share a vocabulary the way two functions can share an argument type without ever calling each other. Level 2B is where that first pays, being the lowest level whose posterior is hidden-state inference rather than a read-off of the observation — inference inside one agent. This component-level inference is distinct from the later coordination of agents by conditional messages.

fig. 2 traces one level from its GNN specification to the live agent and back through the conformance check that binds them. The loop is closed in both directions: beyond being checked against the live agent, every specification also constructs one. ailm.spec_agent.build_agent_from_spec reads the dimensions, counts, slot roles, and parameterization forms from the spec and assembles the pymdp agent, resolving each Learned(generator=..., artifact=...) declaration through an explicit default-deny registry backed by the required corpus artifacts, rather than executing whatever path the spec names — a registered provenance annotated on the wrong slot is refused at construction, which turns the anti-informative wiring of fig. 6 from a conformance violation into a model that cannot be built at all. For every shipped level the spec-built agent is bit-identical — shapes, dtypes, and bytes across every matrix — to the agent the builder functions construct, so the specification and the code provably describe one model rather than two sources of truth that happen to agree (decision 20). That equality is asserted per level in tests/test_spec_agent.py, together with the controls that keep it falsifiable: a planted perturbation, a dtype change, and a missing slot must each make the comparator fail. fig. 3 puts the Part-A models side by side with the alphabet identity that joins L2B to L1 — the composition seam the rest of the stack repeats. The full 6-level stack is drawn in fig. 1, and fig. 22 plots L1→L2B and L3→L2B, the measured channels that share a receiver; sec. 4.10 reports all seven registered interventions. docs/gnn_composition.md works through representational, structural, and planned composition at length.

update_empirical_prior is within-level machinery. Every call site in src/, outside the pymdp API smoke probes, pushes a level’s own posterior through that same level’s own \(\mathbf{B}\) to form the prior for its own next symbol — the second half of eq. 6, staying inside a single agent. The probes in src/ailm/generative/smoke.py are an exception: they call it on placeholder arrays with no level behind them, only to establish which call signature the installed pymdp exposes. That temporal API is not itself an inter-level channel. The historical standalone score paths run one level at a time; the connected runtime adds separate, explicit message transformations rather than redefining update_empirical_prior as a coupling operation. This boundary is tested by five inter-level experiments, each measured separately. A genuine Level 1 to Level 2 message was implemented and measured, and it made the system significantly worse; sec. 6.1 reports the result and its controls, while sec. 4.10 shows a lexical channel into that same level helps substantially when it carries information the level lacks. The L3→L1g generation seam runs top-down instead: sec. 4.9 gives the letter level a controllable transition and sets its \(\mathbf{C}\) from the word level’s lexicon, selecting actions under eq. 2. Separately again, the narrative level’s phase prediction moves the clause level’s joint \(\mathbf{D}\) prior, with an exact zero-weight anchor and a scrambled control (sec. 4.8); this intervention does not use the generator’s \(\mathbf{C}\) mechanism. The privileged punctuation-type-oracle→L3 word-prior intervention is separate again, and it does not consume an L5 posterior. None of these five experiments passes its output into the next. One further caution applies to two of them: the privileged-label arm of the retained case-only clause ablation is evidence of low receiver sensitivity, not a hard bound on the L6→L5 intervention, and both that arm and the intervention are measured against the case-only clause model rather than against the widened one that sec. 5.7.3 promotes.

4.1.4 Worked filtering step: prior to posterior

fig. 4 traces a single symbol through a filtering path. The prior over the current state is the previous posterior pushed through \(\mathbf{B}\); the observation is scored against that prior through \(\mathbf{A}\), which is what eq. 7 measures; the posterior is the normalized product; and the posterior is then pushed through \(\mathbf{B}\) again to become the next prior. The whole cycle is the two halves of eq. 6 and nothing else. L1 executes its headline path through live pymdp. L2A’s canonical full-dictionary score collapses the same recursion to exact initial-phone and bigram sufficient statistics after a bounded live-pymdp/NumPy agreement check; L2B’s full-set scorer implements it in NumPy after a bounded live check with 0 decision disagreements. L4’s full scorer implements the cycle in NumPy, and the live-pymdp recursion is compared with it at every held-out position (sec. 4.6). L3’s exact path score, L5’s closed-form mixture, and L6’s registered observed-position score do not execute this live-agent loop; L5’s live recursion is separately checked against the NumPy joint filter on the full held-out set at the posterior level (sec. 4.7). L6’s separately reported descriptive filter does execute it, but measures sequential prediction from the Agent’s inferred prior rather than the registered known-position conditional.

Locating \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) in that cycle explains why their placement is not interchangeable, and why getting it wrong produces a model that runs.

fig. 5 makes the cycle concrete across the displayed levels: one held-out sentence, traced through the model-specific explanatory paths — the belief state drawn as a heatmap column per position at L1 through L4, and as a scalar type-posterior trace at L5. This visualization does not imply that all panels are recorded by live pymdp inference. Each panel runs on its own index, since the levels do not share one: letters at L1, the letters of a single word at L2B and at L3, tokens at L4, and the case-role prefix at L5. L6 is absent by construction rather than by omission — its observation stream is the sentence-type sequence across a document, so one sentence gives it a single observation and nothing to condition on (sec. 4.8).

4.1.5 Transition statistics and emission semantics

Proposition 2 (Sequence statistics belong in \(\mathbf{B}\)). Let \(M\) be a learned matrix with \(M_{ij} = p(x_{t+1} = i \mid x_t = j)\). Placing \(M\) in the transition slot, \(\mathbf{B} = M\), with \(\mathbf{A} = I\), yields a filtering recursion whose predictive prior is \(\rho_{t+1} = M q_t\), so the model predicts the next symbol from the current one. Placing \(M\) in the emission slot instead, \(\mathbf{A} = M\) with \(\mathbf{B} = I\), yields a posterior \(q_t(j) \propto M_{o_t j}\), which is a distribution over the symbol that \(o_t\); an identity transition then carries that backward-looking belief forward as the prediction for \(o_{t+1}\). Both placements satisfy column-stochasticity, so both are accepted by pymdp’s validator, and only the first is informative.

The wrong placement is quiet rather than loud, which is why it is kept in the suite as a live negative control rather than merely described: the mis-wired agent constructs, validates, performs inference, and returns a finite perplexity throughout. Measured on held-out prose it scores 27.2499 against 11.9215 for the correct wiring — informative enough to clear a threshold badly placed at the uniform baseline of 30, and anti-informative enough to fall well short of the context-free unigram bar at 19.9558, which is the comparator the negative control is actually held to. fig. 6 puts the transition and emission placements side by side; docs/decisions.md records the measurement and the named mis-wirings it generalizes to.

Two consequences shape the rest of the system. First, orientation must be asserted by index, not inferred from a passing validator. The gate tests pin that a lopsided count lands in B[0, next, current, 0] and not its transpose, and they assert normalization along the specific axis that indexes the produced variable — because a transposed matrix still sums to one along some axis. Second, and more general, structural checks cannot catch this class of defect at all. What caught it instead was numerical disagreement with an independently written closed-form chain. That is why src/ailm/verification/oracle.py exists, and why it is forbidden from importing pymdp. sec. 4.11 develops the point.

4.1.6 Tracing a prediction through named matrix entries

The claim that a prediction is answered by naming a column and reading it is worth demonstrating once, on real numbers. Take the letter level at the moment it has just observed q. Three steps close the question. Name the state: the emission is the identity, so the posterior over the current state is q and nothing else. Name the column: q sits at index 20 of the sorted 30-symbol alphabet, so by eq. 6 the prediction for the next symbol is B[0, :, 20, 0]. Read it: the three largest entries are u at 0.9758, space at 0.0095 and period at 0.0051, and the column sums to 1, so nothing has been renormalized for display. Each of those entries is a Laplace-smoothed relative frequency of the corresponding Brown bigram: a count of how often q was followed by that symbol, over a count of how often q occurred. The model predicts u because the number in that cell is 0.9758, and a reader who knows how q behaves in English can judge whether that parameter is the belief it ought to be. That last point is the one worth keeping. The audit is available to a reader, not only to an author with the training run in hand.

Near-determinism is not typical, and quoting only q would imply it is. The column for t is the ordinary case: h at 0.3067, then space at 0.2031 and i at 0.0988 — a real distribution over successors, and a correspondingly weaker prediction. What is identical in the two cases is the procedure: the same three steps, the same named column, read directly off the matrix that a reader can open. scripts/record_worked_example_claims.py recomputes both columns from the vendored counts, so every number in these two paragraphs is a recorded measurement rather than an illustration.

4.1.7 Level factorization and conditioning variables

The alternative to a stack is one agent whose hidden state is the joint of every level’s factor — a single instance of eq. 3 over the product space. Its emission would have \(\lvert O \rvert \prod_f \lvert S_f \rvert\) entries, the product running over every hidden factor, so the joint letter-phoneme-word emission grows in proportion to the size of the vocabulary. A flat factor over every base word in CMUdict is not merely slow to work with; the transition matrix for that factor is quadratic in the vocabulary and exceeds any reasonable storage budget by orders of magnitude, and the joint emission with the phoneme and letter factors multiplies that figure again. The scale table in docs/design/architecture.md records the arithmetic for each level.

Two mechanisms avoid it. Between levels, each level is a separate agent over a separate hidden-factor set, so its matrices are sized by that set alone rather than by the product of every factor beneath it. The interface between Levels 1 and 2 is an alphabet of 30 symbols and the 30 × 39 emission defined over it — not a joint letter-phoneme state space, which is the object whose size the stack exists to avoid ever forming. Within a level, A_dependencies declares which hidden factors each observation modality actually depends on, so pymdp builds one low-dimensional array per modality instead of a single array indexed by every factor jointly. A modality that reads only its own factor gets a three-dimensional array of batch, observation, and state, regardless of how many other factors the level carries. tests/test_pymdp_smoke.py::TestADependenciesShape asserts the resulting shapes, so the factorization is a tested property of the build rather than an assumption about the library.

The word level is where this stops being an optimization. The design document specified a word as a path through a letter-phoneme trie: the state space would be trie positions, and the transition would be the trie’s own branching structure. That alternative was measured rather than argued away. A dense pymdp transition over those trie nodes is 24.6 GB at the length-matched Level 2B vocabulary, and roughly 0.37 TB at full CMUdict. No sparse path is reachable through pymdp’s public Agent API, so this is a representation that does not fit, not a representation that is merely slow. The boundary sits at the API rather than in the mathematics: pymdp’s JAX numerical backend (Bradbury et al. 2018) contains sparse contraction machinery, and the transition contraction this level needs is already sparse-capable, but Agent rejects sparse arrays at construction and does not preserve sparsity across the filtering loop (sec. 12). The shipped level factorizes instead. Its hidden state is word identity × position within the word, and both transitions are structural constants. The trie is not discarded; it is induced: after a prefix, the posterior over the word factor is supported on exactly the vocabulary words carrying that prefix, and that support set is the trie node. This factorized level is the one that is built, and its gate is verified bracketed — see sec. 4.5.

4.1.8 Parameter counts and structural constraints

The factorization argument above is about what a flat model would cost. This is what the shipped one does cost, counted from the built agents rather than from the design: ailm.parameters constructs every level through its own shipped builder and counts three things per array, because any one of them alone points in the wrong direction.

Stored is the dense entry count, what pymdp holds and what sec. 12 prices in bytes. Nonzero is the entries the model can place mass on; the rest are structural zeros fixed by the lexicon and the trie, never estimated from anything. Free is simplex capacity on the live support: every distribution loses one degree of freedom to the simplex constraint, so a column with \(k\) live entries carries \(k - 1\), and a deterministic column carries none. A one-hot emission is a lookup table written as a matrix — it has entries and it has no freedom. This per-array rule does not distinguish fitted distributions from builder-fixed distributions with the same support: Level 1’s uniform start prior contributes simplex capacity although the corpus does not fit it. It also does not infer constraints shared across arrays.

Table 5: Parameters of the historical filtering components, counted from their built agents. The rows are the 7 filtering-agent variants across the six levels of sec. 4.1: Level 2 contributes two, a phoneme sequence model and a letter-to-phone model, and they are listed separately because they are separate agents with separate matrices. Preference vectors are excluded from every column and total 150 entries: C does not normalize, nothing estimates it from a corpus, and folding a preference into a parameter count would inflate the model by an amount carrying no information about the data. Each array’s orientation is asserted before it is counted — a count summed over the wrong axis is wrong without looking wrong, which is the recurring defect sec. 4.11 guards elsewhere. Every level is declared as a GNN file, and the Declared in column is that file. For these historical component builders, the declarations and builders are independently authored, so ailm.parameters checks each built array against the size its spec declares; the counted components conform exactly. The connected runtime instead constructs its six filtering agents from GNN declarations. This census does not count the complete connected runtime: its additional channel and lexical UPOS-encoder arrays are outside these totals. The generation variant of Level 1 has its own spec, gnn/models/L1g_letter_generation.gnn.md, and is not a row here because it is not part of the filtering stack. Level Declared in Stored Nonzero Free
L1 letters gnn/models/L1_letter.gnn.md 1830 960 899
L2A phonemes gnn/models/L2a_phoneme_sequence.gnn.md 3081 1599 1520
L2B letter-to-phone gnn/models/L2b_grapheme_to_phoneme.gnn.md 2730 2730 2651
L3 words gnn/models/L3_word.gnn.md 5136462 46022 1999
L4 case roles gnn/models/L4_case.gnn.md 168 168 151

Total — 5,144,909 51,731 7424

Three things in tbl. 5 are worth reading directly. First, these counted filtering components together have 7424 free parameters, and that is the number this architecture is built to make small enough to inspect by hand. Of the three columns, free describes the capacity remaining after support and normalization constraints. It is not a count of parameters trained by the shipped pipeline, and it is not a directly comparable neural-model parameter count. The reason is that this model declares what a network would have to learn: the 30-symbol letter alphabet, the 39-phone inventory, the 8 case roles borrowed from CEREBRUM, the deterministic spelling table that is the lexicon, the structural zeros, and the builder code that decides which entries exist at all. These counts do not price the information carried by the chosen alphabets, lexicon, role meanings, or builder code. The deterministic spelling table and structural zeros do contribute to the stored and non-zero columns, but they contribute no live-support freedom. The free count also includes the capacity of the fixed uniform start prior, so it does not state how much a corpus decides. Second, only 1.0055% of the stored entries are non-zero, so most of the dense allocation holds structural zeros. Third, the largest dense array belongs to a level with few free values: Level 3 stores 5,136,462 entries, of which 1999 independent probability values are carried by its word unigram prior. Its word transition is an identity padded out to the square of the vocabulary, and its emission gives one letter per word-position pair. The corpus also determines the retained vocabulary and its spelling and length structure, but those contributions are not a count of fitted probabilities.

The factorization makes these independence and deterministic assumptions explicit. An unrestricted learned joint transition over word and position would admit additional degrees of freedom. A dense joint matrix can also encode the same stipulated structure, however, so dense storage alone does not imply that every entry must be estimated. The table counts the shipped design; it does not establish factorization as the only representation of that design.

4.2 Gate taxonomy, threshold placement, and controls

A staged build is only as good as its gates. The premise of the construction in sec. 4.1 — that Stage \(N+1\) may not begin until Stage \(N\) passes a falsifiable test — buys nothing if the test cannot be failed, and buys less than nothing if it cannot be passed, because then the honest response to a correct implementation is indistinguishable from the response to a broken one.

This project shipped both failure modes. They are opposites, they were introduced by the same kind of inattention, and neither was caught by any test, review, or validator. That symmetry is the substance of the audit in sec. 10.1: the two defects are not two mistakes but two halves of one missing check.

4.2.1 Vacuous, unreachable, and discriminating thresholds
