A gate is a threshold together with a direction. Write \(x \succeq t\) for “the measurement \(x\) satisfies the threshold \(t\) as declared”, and \(x \succ t\) for the strict form the audit applies:

\[x \succeq t \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \begin{cases} x \le t, & \text{lower is better (perplexity, error),}\\ x \ge t, & \text{higher is better (accuracy, agreement),} \end{cases} \qquad x \succ t \;\Longleftrightarrow\; x \succeq t \ \text{and}\ x \ne t .\qquad{(10)}\]

The inclusive relation is what every declared threshold’s own wording — >=2 nats above uniform, >=60% — means by “pass”. The strict relation is what the audit uses, and it is exactly the semantics gate_passes in src/ailm/gates.py implements: equality fails in both directions, so a baseline sitting exactly on the bar is never certified vacuous and a typed comparator sitting exactly on the bar never certifies reachability. The two relations disagree only on the boundary \(x = t\) — and that boundary is not an edge case here, it is where every audited row sits. scripts/audit_gates.py sets each row’s threshold to its measured baseline, so \(b_P = t\) exactly, by construction. Under \(\succeq\) every such baseline would “pass” its own bar and every audited gate would be reported vacuous; under \(\succ\) none does. The strict relation is what makes the audit report anything at all, and the price is stated below: with the bar on the baseline, the vacuity half of a bracketed verdict is true by construction and the verdict carries exactly one measured comparison.

Two further quantities are needed, and the whole argument is that they must be measured rather than assumed. The trivial baseline \(b\) is what a model that does none of the work the stage is supposed to demonstrate already scores — for a sequence model, the context-free unigram distribution; for a classification task, a per-item lookup table. The typed comparator is a pair \(c = (c_{\text{value}}, c_{\text{type}})\): a measured or derived comparator together with a declaration of what kind of quantity it is, because the verdicts below differ in what they license and the license comes entirely from the type. The four types this project uses are those of tbl. 22: a model-class bound (a theorem-backed upper bound on every model of the class, on the scored population), an analytic bound (a closed-form bound needing no measurement, such as a total-variation distance of zero), a privileged oracle (a measured comparator given information the model forgoes), and a reference model (a measured system with no privileged access). The first two are bound types; the last two are exceedable types, and the Stage 4 derived row — where the shipped agent scores above its own smoothing reference — is the recorded proof that exceedable comparators are exceeded in practice.

Definition 3 (Threshold placement). Let \(t\) be a threshold whose direction fixes the relations \(\succeq\) and \(\succ\) above, let \(b\) be the measured score of the trivial baseline, and let \(c = (c_{\text{value}}, c_{\text{type}})\) be the typed comparator. Then the gate is if \(b \succ t\); otherwise, if \(c_{\text{value}} \nsucc t\), it is when \(c_{\text{type}}\) is a bound and when \(c_{\text{type}}\) is exceedable; and if \(c_{\text{value}} \succ t\), it is or by the same split. A bracketed gate of either strength is one the trivial baseline strictly fails and the comparator strictly clears, so that passing it is evidence about the model rather than about the threshold; only the bound-typed verdicts assert anything about models other than the ones that were measured.

The typing is the load-bearing repair in this definition, and it was forced by an external audit of an earlier version in which a single untyped \(c\) licensed UNREACHABLE whenever it failed to clear \(t\). That inference is not valid for an exceedable comparator: \[c_{\text{reference}} \nsucc t \quad\not\Rightarrow\quad \sup_{m \in \mathcal{M}} \operatorname{score}(m) \nsucc t,\qquad{(11)}\] because a reference is one member of the admissible class, not its supremum. Only a genuine bound — information-theoretic, analytic, or exhaustive — turns “the comparator fails the bar” into “no implementation can pass”. The classifier therefore refuses an untyped comparator outright (classify_gate in src/ailm/gates.py fails closed), and the licensing rule is machine-checked: unreachable_requires_bound in formal/AILM/GateVerdict.lean proves that UNREACHABLE is derivable only from a bound-typed comparator, whatever the numbers are, and its dual proves a bound is never softened into a reference statement.

The verdict is deliberately named for what it checks. Bracketed is a placement audit and nothing more: it says the measured baseline strictly fails the threshold, and the typed comparator strictly clears it, on a stated population. It does not say the metric is the right one. It does not say the comparator is the strongest available. It does not say the sample is representative. It does not say the effect is large enough to matter. It does not say the threshold was fixed before the run. This paper found several of those conditions violated somewhere in its own work: a defensible-but-not-strongest comparator (sec. 10.1.6), an unrepresentative subsample (sec. 10.1), and a retrospectively re-scoped threshold (tbl. 22). That is exactly why bracketed is not called sound. A gate worth calling scientifically valid needs seven things: a valid construct, a relevant metric, the strongest available comparator, a declared minimum effect, adequate power, a representative test population, and a prospective freeze. The taxonomy here audits one of those seven. The strongest available comparator clause also has a methodological reading this project does not yet meet. That reading would make the comparator search part of the formal method itself: declare the admissible information class, fit its strongest member on training data only, freeze it, and gate against that frozen artifact. Doing so would remove the residual discretion in which comparator gets declared — sec. 10.1.6 shows what that discretion cost at Stage 2B. That change belongs to the analysis code rather than to this paper, and it is recorded here as the standard the next gate revision should meet.

Equivalently, as the classification scripts/audit_gates.py computes, with the verdict indexed by the evaluation population \(P\):

\[\operatorname{verdict}(t; P) = \begin{cases} \text{VACUOUS} & \text{if } b_P \succ t,\\ \text{UNREACHABLE} & \text{if } c_{P} \nsucc t \text{ and } c_{\text{type}} \text{ is a bound,}\\ \text{ABOVE\_REFERENCE} & \text{if } c_{P} \nsucc t \text{ and } c_{\text{type}} \text{ is exceedable,}\\ \text{BRACKETED\_BOUND} & \text{if } c_{P} \succ t \text{ and } c_{\text{type}} \text{ is a bound,}\\ \text{BRACKETED\_REFERENCE} & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}\qquad{(12)}\]

where \(b_P\) and \(c_P\) are the trivial baseline and typed comparator measured on \(P\). The comparator’s type is load-bearing, not annotation: a bound type that fails the bar makes the gate UNREACHABLE and licenses an impossibility claim, while an exceedable type that fails it makes the gate ABOVE_REFERENCE and licenses none; a bound type that clears the bar brackets the model as BRACKETED_BOUND, and an exceedable one that clears it is the ordinary BRACKETED_REFERENCE comparison. The case analysis the audit applies to the declared thresholds is set out in sec. 10. Step 4 of the pre-build checklist (sec. 10) makes the population index a requirement rather than a notation, and the Stage 1 row is where it bit: its comparator was the Brown training conditional entropy while its baseline and model were scored on held-out prose, so the single comparison a baseline-relative verdict contains straddled two populations. scripts/audit_gates.py now uses that passage’s own empirical order-1 optimum, 5.9928 (the perplexity of the all-position bound of eq. 21), which is the same quantity measured where the gate is scored. The population index is not decoration; it is this section’s own Stage 4 lesson stated in its own notation: \(\operatorname{verdict}(t; P_{\text{gold}}) = \text{VACUOUS}\) while \(\operatorname{verdict}(t; P_{\text{derived}}) = \text{ABOVE\_REFERENCE}\) at the same \(t\) (sec. 10.1.5) — above-reference and not unreachable, because the derived population’s comparators are a smoothing decode and a test-fitted lookup, both exceedable, so no impossibility claim is licensed there. A verdict is a property of the pair \((t, P)\), never of \(t\) alone — which is why audit_stage4() in scripts/audit_gates.py takes population as a parameter instead of baking one in.

The order of the cases in eq. 12 is not arbitrary. Under the strict relation, VACUOUS and the failing-comparator verdicts cannot co-fire whenever \(c_P \succeq b_P\): if \(b_P \succ t\) and \(c_P \succeq b_P\), then \(c_P \succ t\), so neither failing case can trigger. Reporting VACUOUS first therefore loses no information and keeps the more actionable diagnosis in front.

The condition \(c_P \succeq b_P\) is measured on every audited row, not assumed. It cannot be justified “by construction, since the comparator bounds every model in the class including the trivial one”, because these values are typed comparators — a smoothing oracle, a conditional entropy, a per-item argmax — and only some of them bound the model class. The Stage 4 derived row is the counterexample in this project’s own ledger, where the shipped agent scores above its recorded smoothing reference. What the case order needs is the weaker fact about the baseline, which holds on every recorded row except the retained case-only clause ablation, where the type oracle scores worse than the type-free baseline (and where, with \(t = b_P\), VACUOUS cannot fire anyway), and is checked there; nothing here needs, or gets, a bound over every model.

One degenerate case is worth naming because the argument above is silent on it: when \(b_P = c_P\) the bracketed region is empty, and no threshold on that population can earn either bracketed verdict — the data admits no gate at all, which is itself a measurement worth having before building the level. This is not a hypothetical shape. The Stage 4 gold population realizes it exactly: its trivial baseline is 63.8%, its smoothing reference 63.8% and the shipped model 63.8% — one number three times (tbl. 25). No threshold scored against that population could discriminate anything, whatever value were chosen, which is why no gate is stated there. The general statement is machine-checked as degenerate_no_gate in formal/AILM/GateVerdict.lean rather than argued in prose.

A consequence of the audit’s own convention deserves stating plainly, because a bracketed verdict otherwise reads as more than it is. Setting \(t := b_P\) makes the first case of eq. 12 never fire: \(b_P \succ b_P\) is false for every population and either direction, so the vacuity test is discharged by the strictness of \(\succ\) rather than by anything measured. On those rows a bracketed verdict is therefore equivalent to \(c_P \succ b_P\) — the comparison that the typed comparator genuinely beats the trivial baseline. That is a real and falsifiable claim about the data, and it is the whole of what every row in the canonical audit inventory asserts; a re-measurement can move a comparator relative to its baseline, but a baseline can never cross a threshold defined to equal it. The equivalence is machine-checked as bracketed_at_baseline_bar_iff in formal/AILM/GateVerdict.lean.

Because a reader meets the verdicts in the audit’s output before meeting this paragraph, the property is named in the code as well: gate_is_baseline_relative in src/ailm/gates.py reports whether a row’s threshold equals its baseline, and scripts/audit_gates.py prints that beside every affected verdict and counts the affected rows in its summary. The predicate is deliberately not an extra verdict. Whether a verdict was predetermined is a fact about how the gate was constructed, not about how the classifier behaves, and the six-way classification is fixed by theorems in the Lean development that a new case would invalidate. What carries evidential weight on a baseline-relative row is therefore not the verdict but the two measurements beside it — that the comparator beats the baseline, and that the shipped model does, the latter reported as the audit’s OUTCOME line and, where the margin is small, backed by a paired test rather than by a bare number.

fig. 7 is the same statement drawn once per gate. The useful property of the picture is that it makes the two defects visibly symmetric — one threshold falls on the wrong side of \(b\), the other on the wrong side of \(c\) — which is not obvious from either defect considered alone.

The audit is also executable rather than narrative. scripts/audit_gates.py re-derives the classification of eq. 12 for every implemented stage on every run, fixes its inventory in AUDITED_GATE_IDS, and exits non-zero when a verdict changes, when the model lands on the wrong side of its own bar, or when a gate stops being audited. The same experience distilled a pre-build checklist — metric and direction fixed in code before any number exists, the trivial baseline and a typed comparator measured on the scored population, the negative control written before the model — that no gate in this project was built under and that is recorded as what the next gate revision should satisfy. The script’s exit conditions, its restatement caveat, and every checklist step are set out in sec. 10.

4.3 Level 1: a letter bigram fitted on Brown against a restated context-free bar

4.3.1 Letter states and Brown corpus counts

This subsection fixes the letter alphabet Level 1 predicts over and names the corpus its transition counts come from.

L1 is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L1_letter.gnn.md fixes the letter transition, the identity emission and the flat start prior; every dimension and slot role in this section is read from it, and tbl. 5 checks the built agent against that declaration. The spec does not generate the builder — both are written by hand, which is why the check is worth running.

Level 1 models a single character at a time. The alphabet in src/ailm/levels/letter.py is lowercase a through z plus space, period, apostrophe, and hyphen, sorted so that indexing is deterministic and every matrix row and column has a fixed meaning across runs. A uniform distribution over that alphabet has perplexity 30, which is the number every subsequent comparison is read against. normalize_text lowercases input and maps every character outside the alphabet to a space, so the model never sees a symbol it has no state for.

The transition is trained on the Brown corpus (Francis and Kučera 1979) and reaches 805 distinct bigram types over 5,856,736 bigram tokens. Normalization is documented in docs/provenance/sources.md and includes two choices that matter: whitespace runs collapse to a single space, and spaces immediately preceding a period or apostrophe are stripped. Brown’s tokenizer emits punctuation as separate tokens, so without those steps the space-space pair would dominate every other bigram and no letter would ever transition directly into a period, which would distort exactly the end-of-word statistics the level is supposed to learn. Counts are vendored as vendor/brown_counts.json (14 kB, sha256 778e2b31740b) and verified byte-identical on regeneration, so the level’s tests need no network access and the training data is pinned rather than described.

4.3.2 Bigram transition matrix

build_letter_transition accumulates the counts into a square matrix with default add-1 smoothing, then normalizes each column so that \(\mathbf{B}_{ij} = p(\text{next} = i \mid \text{current} = j)\). Smoothing is not cosmetic: without it, the matrix would assign zero probability to any legal English pair absent from Brown, driving eq. 7 to infinity on held-out text. build_letter_agent then places that matrix in the transition slot and sets the emission to the identity, since observing a letter reveals the letter state exactly. fig. 8 shows the result.

Every entry of that matrix is a named conditional probability, and the whole of the level’s behavior is a lookup in it. There is nothing else in the level to interpret.

4.4 Level 2: a phoneme chain and a position-aligned letter-to-phone decoder

Level 2 holds a phone-sequence model and a letter-to-phone model, and the distinction between them is the point of the level. Part A is the letter level one rung down: a sequence model over phones, emission the identity, dynamics in the transition. Part B is the first level whose emission is not the identity — letters are observed, phones are hidden, and A is a learned letter-given-phone matrix. That makes Part B’s posterior an inference rather than a read-off of the observation. It does not make it a message from one agent to another; sec. 4.1 keeps those two senses of hierarchical apart, and only the first is claimed here. Both live in src/ailm/levels/phoneme.py.

L2 is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L2a_phoneme_sequence.gnn.md fixes the phoneme sequence model; the letter-to-phone model beside it is declared in gnn/models/L2b_grapheme_to_phoneme.gnn.md; every dimension and slot role in this section is read from them, and tbl. 5 checks each built agent against its declaration. The spec does not generate the builder — both are written by hand, which is why the check is worth running.

The inventory is the 39 canonical ARPAbet phones with stress digits stripped, sourced from CANONICAL_ARPABET in src/ailm/corpus/cmudict.py. The source contributes 135,166 pronunciation entries for 126,052 base words. The inventory count is an enforced invariant rather than a constant: naive whitespace splitting of CMUdict (Carnegie Mellon University Speech Group, n.d.) yields 54 distinct tokens, including 15 comment-only phantoms after #; stripping comments recovers the canonical 39. A negative control asserts that the naive path fails the count. All Stage 2 inputs are derived into vendor/cmudict_counts.json (978 kB, sha256 9f0f20746086), verified byte-identical on regeneration and checked against the file on disk by tests/test_provenance_checksums.py — a documented checksum that has drifted from its artifact is worse than no checksum.

4.4.1 Part A: phoneme bigram chain

build_phone_transition estimates \(\mathbf{B}_{ij} = p(\text{next phone} = i \mid \text{current phone} = j)\) from the primary pronunciation of every CMUdict base word, and build_phone_unigram supplies \(\mathbf{D}\), the distribution over word-initial phones. The prior resets to \(\mathbf{D}\) at each word boundary. That is a modeling decision with a measured justification. The alternative treats the dictionary as one continuous phone stream, predicting each word’s first phone from the previous word’s last phone. It measures worse than paying the unigram price at position zero, because there is no dependency across a word boundary to exploit. Position zero has no predecessor and is charged for accordingly.

Part A is computed in closed form over all 800,198 positions of the dictionary, and never over the length-matched subset that Part B requires. The two are measurements of different populations. That subset selects words whose letter and phone counts coincide, which biases it toward short words with transparent orthography and, as Part B’s alignment subsection sets out, pairs even those words by index rather than by correspondence. So no whole-dictionary claim can be read off it in either direction, and the size of the discrepancy is not predictable from the selection rule. sec. 10.1 quantifies the gap.

4.4.2 Part B: position-aligned letter-to-phone decoding

Part B observes letters and infers phones, on words whose letter count equals their phone count, pairing the two sequences by index. The name of the task is that sentence: equal-length position-aligned letter-to-phone decoding. It is not grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, and the matrix it learns is not a grapheme-to-phoneme alignment. The next subsection says exactly what the index pairing does and does not buy, and the label is used consistently from here on because phoneme prediction and position-aligned letter-to-phone decoding have different targets, not merely different difficulty.

The shipped builders, the GNN specification file and every recorded claim label at this level nevertheless carry the string g2p. Those names are the implementation’s, fixed before the task was named correctly, and the construct they denote is the one this subsection names. They are left unchanged because a claim label is an identifier that the ledger, the tests and the specification registry resolve, not a description of a construct; renaming them would break the single-writer discipline that makes every number here traceable, in exchange for a word. Level 6 carries the same split for the same reason (sec. 4.8), and the rule is the same in both places: read the identifier as a key, and the surrounding sentence as the claim.

build_g2p_emission estimates \(\mathbf{A}_{lp} = p(\text{letter } l \mid \text{phone } p)\) over co-indexed pairs, column-stochastic over letters for each phone; build_g2p_transition estimates the phone bigram on the training split only; build_g2p_start supplies the distribution over first phones. decode_phonemes then runs eq. 6 one letter at a time and takes the posterior mode at each position. This is the first level whose emission carries information, and therefore the first level where the inference does real work rather than reading the state off the observation. fig. 9 shows both learned matrices side by side; their differing shapes are the visible form of the point sec. 4.1 argues structurally.

4.4.2.1 Alignment restriction and excluded corpus coverage

Learning \(p(\text{letter} \mid \text{phone})\) requires knowing which letter emitted which phone, and CMUdict does not say. Equal letter and phone counts make the index pairing unique — zip the equal-length sequences and every letter has exactly one partner, with no insertion or deletion left to place. They do not make those pairs grapheme-to-phoneme correspondences. English spells a phone with a digraph, spells multiple phones with a single letter, and leaves letters silent, so a word can carry as many letters as phones and still require a many-to-many alignment. use = Y UW S has three of each, and the index pairing counts u→Y, s→UW, e→S; all three are wrong, because u spells Y UW together, s spells S, and e is silent. one = W AH N counts o→W, n→AH, e→N, and is wrong the same way. Both words sit in the training half of the split, so those counts are in the shipped matrix.

The consequence runs deeper than a biased sample. The learned emission can encode systematically wrong local correspondences on words the selection rule admits, which fixes what \(\mathbf{A}\) is: a statistical relation between co-indexed symbols, not a learned grapheme-to-phoneme alignment. The G2P literature treats alignment as a latent many-to-many problem for exactly this reason, and joint-sequence models over graphone units are its classical probabilistic answer (Bisani and Ney 2008). AILM does not answer it. It declines to guess an alignment on unequal-length words, because a guessed alignment is fabricated training data, and it declines to run expectation maximization, which is a research contribution with its own convergence diagnostics and held-out likelihood check and cannot be smuggled into a level gate as a preprocessing step. What is left is the index pairing on the length-matched subset — a stipulation rather than a discovery, and the level is scoped to it.

The rest of the cost is stated rather than absorbed. The length-matched subset is 25.7% of the dictionary (25,936 training and 6484 held-out pairs). It is held out by a stride over the sorted pair list: every fifth index is test and the rest are train, so the split is reproducible from the artifact with no seed to record. The stride matters and is worth stating explicitly rather than leaving to the word sorted. The list is alphabetical, so a contiguous cut would put whole initial-letter neighborhoods on one side, while an interleave distributes them. It does: the initial-letter distributions of the two sides differ by 0.00085 in total variation. What the interleave does not remove is morphological neighbors: 82.5% of held-out words share a 4-character prefix with some training word. On a task whose whole subject is letter-to-phone regularity, that overlap is partly the phenomenon rather than contamination. Still, it bounds how independent the held-out score is, and it is recorded here rather than left for a reader to infer. 74.3% of the dictionary is discarded, and not at random: length-matched words skew short, skew transparent, and skew away from silent letters, digraphs, and vowel clusters. through and knight are excluded; cat, stop, and plant are not. Every accuracy figure below is therefore a claim about position-aligned letter-to-phone decoding on that subset. It is not a claim about grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, and it is not a claim about English. Reconstructing the same subset would still not make it comparable with a published G2P system, because such a system predicts a word’s pronunciation while Part B predicts the phone co-indexed with each letter under a pairing the evaluation itself imposes. sec. 6.1 carries this forward as the sharpest restriction on the level’s generality.

4.5 Level 3: a word level factored into identity and position

Level 3 is where the design document’s specification stopped being implementable. Words were to be paths through a letter–phoneme trie, with the transition encoding trie-constrained letter steps. Measured over the length-matched letter-to-phone vocabulary, that trie has 78,398 nodes and 78,397 edges, so a dense pymdp transition over trie nodes is 24.6 GB at float32 and 0.0013% occupied; extrapolated to full CMUdict it is roughly 0.37 TB. No sparse path is reachable through pymdp.agent.Agent’s public API. That is a statement about the API and not about the mathematics, and the difference is worth stating because the shorter claim — that pymdp has no sparse path — is false: its JAX backend contains sparse contraction machinery, and the transition contraction this level uses is already sparse-capable. What Agent does is reject sparse arrays at construction and lose sparsity across the filtering loop. Under two patches at those two sites a sparse-transition agent reproduces the dense agent’s posteriors exactly, which is what makes the restriction an interface boundary rather than a limit of the method. This is not a performance problem to optimize but a representation that does not fit, and the distinction matters: the response to the first is tuning, and the response to the second is a design decision that has to be recorded with its rejected alternatives.

L3 is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L3_word.gnn.md fixes both hidden factors, word identity and position within the word, and the emission over letters; every dimension and slot role in this section is read from it, and tbl. 5 checks the built agent against that declaration. The spec does not generate the builder — both are written by hand, which is why the check is worth running.

4.5.1 Word identity and position factorization

The shipped level factorizes the hidden state into two pymdp factors — word identity over a bounded vocabulary of 2000 types, and position within the word — with a single letter modality depending on both through A_dependencies = [[0, 1]]. The emission is deterministic: A[k, w, p] is one exactly when letter p of word w is symbol k, or when k is the end-of-word symbol and p has passed the word’s last letter. B over word identity is the identity matrix — a word does not become a different word part-way through being spelled — and B over position is the +1 shift.

The trie is not discarded, it is induced. After observing a prefix, the posterior over the word factor is supported on exactly the vocabulary words carrying that prefix, which is the trie node. That correspondence is checked against a live agent rather than argued: test_posterior_support_is_the_trie_node compares the posterior’s support against the set of vocabulary words carrying each prefix, and a companion test confirms the support genuinely narrows as the prefix lengthens, so the equality cannot pass by returning everything.

What those tests establish is prefix-support equivalence, and the claim is stated at that strength deliberately. The map from a factored state \((w, t)\) to the trie node for the prefix \(w_{1:t}\) is many-to-one — every word sharing a prefix lands on one node — so it is a projection rather than a change of coordinates, and the factored level retains a word identity the node has already aggregated away. Promoting the correspondence to equivalence of the two stochastic processes would require showing the projection is a lumping: that the prefix partition is a probabilistic bisimulation, with each node’s mass equal to the summed prior mass of the words it aggregates and the trie’s transition equal to the pushforward of the factored one. This project neither proves that nor relies on it; every measurement below is stated over the factored model. fig. 10 shows the level’s matrices and fig. 11 the narrowing they produce.

The factorization is also cheaper by an order of magnitude for the same vocabulary and the same coverage, because it spends states on words rather than on prefixes. It puts word identity in the model explicitly, which is what a word level ought to have — under the trie encoding the word is recoverable only by asking which terminal node was reached.

Because every factor except the word prior is deterministic, the probability the model assigns to a word’s full emission path collapses exactly to that word’s unigram probability. That identity is the level’s load-bearing invariant, and sec. 10.1.4 is where it earns that description.

4.5.2 Vocabulary scope and closed-form extension

The vocabulary bound is a scoping decision, not a tuning parameter. 76.4% of held-out alphabetic Brown tokens are in vocabulary; the model assigns the remainder no probability at all, not a small one, and every number in this section describes that sublanguage. The functions refuse to score an out-of-vocabulary token rather than falling back to a smoothed value, because a smoothed number would report a result for an input the model is undefined on.

The corpus population is partitioned before frequency fitting by a category-stratified, revision-bound hash of whole-document identities. Of 500 authenticated Brown source documents, 448 train and 52 are held out, with 0 document overlap. Both derived artifacts retain the ordered file identities, their length-framed digest, the exhaustive split, and a document index for every evaluation token; the loaders reject a duplicate, cross-arm alias, category relabeling, count drift, or token mapped outside the held-out arm. All 15 Brown categories contribute: 15 are represented in training and 15 in evaluation, so the corpus’s genre-blocked file order cannot collapse evaluation onto its last genres. Thus the word-frequency prior and its evaluation population are source-document disjoint and genre-stratified, not merely token-position disjoint.

The refusal to score out-of-vocabulary tokens is correct and it has a cost, and until the complete held-out stream was vendored the cost could not be measured. vendor/brown_word_counts.json carries the evaluation stream already filtered to the lexicon, so the tokens the level excludes were absent from the repository entirely and the coverage figure above was a definition rather than a measurement. vendor/brown_heldout_stream.json is the unfiltered denominator — 102,404 tokens over 12,930 types, of which 24,163 (23.595757978203977%) fall outside the lexicon — and filtering it to the lexicon reproduces the shipped evaluation stream element-for-element, which is asserted as a test rather than assumed.

What it shows is that coverage selects an easier population, and the comparator is what shows it. The letter-bigram bar is defined on any alphabetic string, so it can be scored where the word level cannot, and scoring one model on three populations isolates the population from the system. It reaches 9.054720916239274 on the covered sublanguage, 10.330468611764502 on the whole held-out stream, and 13.27373940157792 on the excluded remainder alone.

The obvious mechanism is length, and it is not the mechanism. Covered tokens average 3.839508697485973 letters against 7.2394984066548025 for excluded ones. That difference invites a simple story: a frequency-ranked lexicon selects short words, and short words are easier for a letter model. Two marginal means cannot support that story, and stratifying by length refutes it. Split the data into 14 length buckets, each holding at least 30 tokens on both sides: the excluded tokens are harder in 12 of those buckets. Next, standardize both per-emission scores to the covered length distribution, weighting each length-\(L\) bucket by its covered token count times \(L+1\) emissions. That gives 9.054720916220827 against 14.80835728699474. Matching on length does not shrink the gap; it widens it, from 0.38250133238192774 nats to 0.4919054330492272, a change of 28.60227962763262%. So on this per-emission estimand, length was masking part of the effect rather than producing it.

What the effect actually is remains unmeasured, and saying so is the honest stopping point. The plausible account is that in-vocabulary tokens are the frequent, orthographically typical ones whose letter transitions dominate the token-weighted counts the comparator is estimated from, so the covered sublanguage is easy for the bar in the same way it is easy for the level. That is a hypothesis this section does not test, and it is recorded as one.

This does not make the Stage 3 comparison wrong. It is a paired comparison on identical tokens, and both systems meet the same easier population. What it does is fix what the comparison is about: the level’s reported gain describes 76.4% of running text, and the 23.595757978203977% it says nothing about is the harder part. The word level is not scored on the excluded tokens under any smoothing rule, here or anywhere, because that would be the smoothed number this section refuses above.

Stage 3 is measured on Brown rather than the Penn Treebank (PTB) the original gate named. The full treebank is licensed through the Linguistic Data Consortium (LDC), and nltk ships only a partial sample under research terms, so a number reported against “PTB” would have named a corpus this project does not have. Brown is already vendored, checksummed and byte-reproducible, and is the corpus Level 1 trains on. All Stage 3 inputs are derived into vendor/brown_word_counts.json, verified byte-identical on regeneration and checked against the file on disk.

4.6 Level 4: case roles inferred over a UD-derived label, scored on both populations

Level 4 assigns each token of a sentence one of the 8 case roles of the CEREBRUM inventory (Friedman 2025). The construct it infers is a syntactic role, not grammatical case. Universal Dependencies English EWT marks case morphologically as Nominative, Accusative and Genitive only, and marks it on pronouns only (Marneffe et al. 2021; Nivre et al. 2020; Silveira et al. 2014): in the split this project vendors, every token carrying feats[Case] is a pronoun. The other 5 roles — dative, instrumental, locative, ablative and vocative — have no morphological ground truth in this corpus in principle, and every label they carry comes from an explicit heuristic over deprel and adposition lemmas. So does every label carried by a non-pronoun in the other 3.

L4 is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L4_case.gnn.md fixes the case-role transition and the learned emission over UPOS tags; every dimension and slot role in this section is read from it, and tbl. 5 checks the built agent against that declaration. The spec does not generate the builder — both are written by hand, which is why the check is worth running.

That most of the inventory has no morphological realization in English is a property of the construct, not a defect of the corpus. The point dates to Fillmore’s case grammar (Fillmore 1968). Fillmore argued that case relationships belong in the base as primitives, and that “subject” and “direct object” are proper only to the surface structure of some languages. His own inventory (agentive, instrumental, dative, factitive, locative, objective, later benefactive) is deliberately semantic: he did not expect English morphology to mark it. Dative, instrumental, and locative are deep cases in Fillmore’s own inventory, and they are among the 5 roles this level carries without morphological ground truth. Ablative is not one of Fillmore’s cases. Vocative cannot be one by his definition, since it is not a relation between a nominal and the predicate. The lineage is therefore partial. The part that transfers is the general point rather than the list: a case inventory can be semantic and still have no morphological realization in a particular language. Naming Fillmore does not license the heuristic used here; it identifies what the heuristic is a heuristic for. That is why the scope of the partial fidelity check below matters rather than being a formality. Fillmore himself later reopened the question of whether a fixed inventory is the right object at all (Fillmore 1977), and this section inherits that caution along with the frame.

The honest description of the level is therefore heuristic syntactic case-role inference over an inventory of 8 roles, 3 of them partly anchored in UD morphology and 5 of them supplied entirely by the heuristic. Naming it that way is what makes the rest of this section measurable rather than merely disclosed. A level claiming grammatical case would have to treat its labels as ground truth and report accuracy against them; a level claiming a labeling scheme can report that scheme’s fidelity against the morphology that does exist, and can state its gate over the population where the scheme actually applies. Both appear below.

The hidden factor is the case role, A is a learned emission \(p(\text{UPOS} \mid \text{case})\), and B is the case-role transition along the sentence. Structurally it is the letter-to-phone model one level up: two different alphabets, observations of one and inference over the other. It is implemented in src/ailm/levels/case.py and evaluated over 2001 sentences and 25,148 tokens from 318 authenticated EWT # newdoc id blocks. Those raw document identities are reconstructed before either label population is filtered. A deterministic stride assigns 254 documents to training and 64 to test, with 0 documents in both arms. Gold and derived populations inherit that one partition; filtering can remove a document from a population, but can never move one across the split.

4.6.1 Case-level observation alphabet

The model observes the token’s universal part-of-speech tag and nothing else. Neither deprel nor feats[Case] reaches it, and the restriction is recorded in the vendored artifact’s own provenance rather than left to the implementation.

The reason is that the evaluation labels are derived from those fields. A model observing deprel would be reading its own answer key: agreement would approach perfect agreement and would measure nothing about case-role structure at all. This is the sharpest trap in the project so far, and it is worth being precise about why. Every earlier mis-wiring made a model worse — anti-informative, collapsed, upside down — and a suspicious number is something a reviewer can pull on. This one makes the model excellent. There is no numeric signature to notice, no degraded score to investigate, and a gate stated purely as a threshold would pass comfortably while certifying a circularity. The only possible guard is structural, so the observation alphabet is checked for what it is not allowed to contain. fig. 12 shows the emission, transition, and start-prior arrays with their cells annotated.

4.6.2 Gold and derived case populations

The gold population is the tokens carrying UD feats[Case]: 3 roles, real English morphology, every one of them a pronoun. The derived population is every token the syntactic heuristic can label, and it is the population Stage 4’s gate is stated over. The two are reported separately because a merged figure would be part measurement and part heuristic with no way to tell which part is which.

The heuristic is a research claim, not ground truth, and its fidelity is measurable: where both labelings exist, over 1752 tokens, the syntactic rules agree with real morphology 89.5% of the time.

That figure is narrower than it looks, and the narrowness is not a caveat but the whole of what it measures. Both labelings exist only on tokens carrying feats[Case], which in English EWT means pronouns, in the 3 morphologically marked roles. The derived test population is 1319 tokens spanning all 8. So the agreement figure checks the heuristic exactly where the corpus can check it, and says nothing about the 5 roles for which this corpus has no morphological ground truth in principle. It is not a bound on the fidelity of the derived labeling as a whole, and reading it as one is the mistake the wording here is built to prevent. The scoring function is named case_agreement rather than case_accuracy so that overstating it takes deliberate effort; the same discipline applies to the fidelity number itself.

The sufficient counts make that boundary executable. Across the full parsed EWT development shard, the oracle labels 7288 tokens: 1798 through morphology, 3898 through the dependency-relation map, and 1592 through the token-level adposition route. The heuristic-versus-gold overlap contains 1752 dependency-route tokens and 0 token-level adposition-route tokens. The reported agreement therefore supplies no fidelity estimate for that adposition route.

That route also exposes a construct duplication rather than a parser accident. It assigns the ADP token from the ADP’s own lemma; it does not look up or relabel the nominal head. None of its 1592 tokens carries gold Case morphology, while 1516 have a head that the oracle separately labels. The ADP-token and head roles disagree in 888 of those pairs (58.58%). This audit preserves the measured labels and gates; it shows why neither the overlap agreement nor an English morphological comparison can decide whether the ADP-token construct is valid. Relabeling the nominal head would define a new research population and would require a new recorded run, not an editorial correction.

Computing that fidelity number correctly required one correction worth recording. The natural implementation calls the project’s own case oracle on each token and compares the result against the gold morphology — but the oracle consults feats[Case] first, so on exactly the tokens being compared it returns the gold label itself. The measurement reads as perfect agreement, green by construction, and confirms nothing. The syntactic rules have to be applied directly, bypassing the morphological shortcut, which is the comparison the number was always supposed to make.

4.7 Level 5: clause type, built on a case-only ablation and a canonical widened alphabet

This section describes the case-only clause model, which is the retained ablation rather than the canonical Level 5. The canonical arm’s alphabet, population and comparators are specified in sec. 4.7.1. The stage5_ ledger prefix stays with the case-only arm. Decision 118 updates tbl. 5 to count the canonical widened agent; the retained ablation is counted separately as 400 stored, 160 nonzero and 127 free entries, excluded from the canonical total.

Its joint hidden state contains sentence type — declarative or interrogative, labeled by the sentence-final punctuation token — together with case role. Its observation alphabet is the same case-role inventory that Level 4 uses as a hidden state, which is the exact identity the canonical arm’s widened alphabet gives up (sec. 6.2). The scored stream is supplied directly by the UD-derived artifact, however; it is not a posterior emitted by a running Level 4 Agent.

This arm is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L5_clause.gnn.md fixes the joint type-by-case state space and its transition. The canonical arm’s gnn/models/L5w_clause_widened.gnn.md declares the wider alphabet and the agent counted in tbl. 5. Both specs are checked against their own built agents, with mutation controls. The specs and builders are independently written. The parameter recorder requires each arm to conform to its own declaration; separate crossed-spec tests require each arm to fail against the other’s declaration.

The construct is that and no more. Sentence type here is a binary latent defined by a single character. The level models no constituent structure, no main-versus-subordinate distinction, no coordination or complementation, and no mood beyond what the final mark encodes; none of those is present in the observation stream, and none could be recovered from it. Calling this a clause level would import four constructs into a measurement that contains none of them. What the measurement does contain — what a punctuation-defined binary is worth to case-role prediction — is a smaller question, and the one this design can answer.

The model is a 2-component mixture of case-role Markov chains, embedded as a single-factor pymdp agent over the joint (type × case) space: 16 states, a block-diagonal transition with zero cross-type mass (a sentence does not change type mid-way, as a word does not drift mid-spelling), a deterministic emission reading off the case component, and a prior \(P(\text{type}) \otimes P(\text{first case} \mid \text{type})\). Filtering a case sequence accumulates evidence about the type; the type posterior is the block marginal. The reported full-set score computes the corresponding mixture evidence in closed form. The live Agent stores the same arrays, and its inference API is equated with the same model on the full held-out set. Over all 178 held-out sentences (1072 positions), the Agent’s infer_states / update_empirical_prior recursion produces the sentence-type posterior argmax with 0 disagreements against the NumPy joint forward filter over the identical matrices, and its full joint (type × case) posterior deviates from that filter by at most 1.67e-07 at any position. The argmax count is not the load-bearing statistic: on this population the filter’s type argmax is the same type at every position, so a transition with no case dynamics at all also scores 0 disagreements while its joint posterior departs from the filter by a wide margin. The posterior tolerance is the check that separates the two, and the recorder refuses to write if either statistic moves. This is posterior agreement between the live inference path and the independent oracle that audits it. It is not score equivalence for the headline mixture estimand, which remains closed-form.

The disjointness discipline of sec. 4.6 applies one level up, and holds structurally: the type label’s source is the punctuation token’s form, the observations are syntactic case roles derived from UD dependency structure, and PUNCT tokens carry no case role — so the label source cannot appear in the observation stream. The artifact generator asserts this at build time, and the observation alphabet is checked to be exactly the 8 case roles. Sentences ending “!” (68) and unpunctuated web fragments (184) carry no label and are excluded, stated rather than smoothed over; every Stage 5 number describes the typed sublanguage of 846 training and 178 held-out sentences. The split is made before those filters: the generator reconstructs all 318 raw EWT # newdoc id blocks, assigns 254 whole documents to training and 64 to test, asserts 0 overlapping documents, and only then retains typed sentences. The retained training sequences come from 196 contributing documents and the test sequences from 53. Thus neither a second sentence from a held-out document nor a filtered sentence from it can leak that document’s identity into model fitting.

4.7.1 Canonical widened observation alphabet

This is the canonical Level 5’s specification. The clause level admits a second observation alphabet, and decision 114 made that one the arm the paper describes. The case-only stream of sec. 4.7 is the derived case-role sequence, which is Level 4’s hidden states read exactly one level down, and that stream cannot represent the two parts of speech that occupy a position in English surface order while carrying no case. The widened arm adds one distinguished symbol for each verb and each auxiliary, taking the alphabet to 10 symbols and the joint state space to 20 states in the same type-major, block-diagonal arrangement. Nothing else about the receiver changes: the recognition matrix remains the deterministic read-off of the symbol component, the transition retains exactly zero cross-type mass, and the prior remains the type prior times each type’s first-symbol distribution. The estimators are the shipped ones, called at the larger alphabet rather than transcribed a second time.

Widening an observation stream toward the label is the failure this level was built to avoid, so the disjointness assertion is strengthened rather than relaxed. Sentence-final punctuation remains the type label’s source and punctuation emits nothing; a verb or auxiliary contributes its part-of-speech tag alone, never its lemma, its morphological features, or its surface form. Both properties are asserted per sentence when the artifact is built, by recomputation rather than by inspection: every punctuation token is offered to the extractor alone and must yield nothing, and the recorded sequence must equal what the extractor produces from a view of the same tokens in which lemma, features and form are replaced by a single shared sentinel. An extraction that consults any withheld field disagrees with itself under that substitution and the build stops. A planted lemma leak and a planted punctuation emitter are both rejected by that assertion in the test suite.

The arm inherits the authenticated document partition before exclusions, so its arms are document-disjoint and its intervals resample whole source documents. One rule genuinely differs and is stated rather than inherited in silence: a sentence is usable here when it contributes at least the minimum number of widened symbols, where the shipped artifact requires that many case-bearing tokens. The two populations are therefore nested rather than equal, and per-position perplexity is never compared between the case-only arm and the widened one. The comparison that is valid across them is a per-sentence statistic about the same binary variable on the same sentences, and that is the one reported.

The arm was specified before its artifact was regenerated. The alphabet, the partition, the receiver, the comparators, the gate, the controls, the predictions and the falsifiers were fixed in advance, and the outcome was not re-selected afterwards. The specification was written within the development session and has no independently timestamped prior artifact, so every quantity it produces is recorded as descriptive and none of its p-values joins the frozen multiplicity family.

4.8 Level 6: document-position terciles, registered before the held-out score

One step up from the sentence sits the document. Level 6’s observation alphabet is the sentence-type component named inside Level 5, and its hidden state is the document-position tercile: the opening, middle or closing third of a document by sentence index. Its scored sequence comes from punctuation-defined corpus labels, not a running Level 5 Agent’s posterior. The shipped code, the figure panels and the recorded claim labels name this variable phase; that name is the implementation’s, and the construct it denotes is the tercile.

L6 is declared as a GNN file. gnn/models/L6_narrative.gnn.md fixes the three document-position terciles and the emission over sentence types; every dimension and slot role in this section is read from it, and tbl. 5 checks the built agent against that declaration. The spec does not generate the builder — both are written by hand, which is why the check is worth running.

The tercile is a position, not a narrative phase. Nothing in this corpus annotates discourse structure, so no measurement here can distinguish an opening third from an exposition, a setup or a lede: the construct is the ordinal partition, not whatever that partition might correlate with. Naming it that way costs the level its most interesting-sounding claim and keeps the one it can test — whether sentence-type probabilities differ by where a sentence sits in its document.

The operationalization is deliberately austere. A tercile is a function of position, so every parameter is a count; there is no expectation-maximization (EM) or fitted latent segmentation. That austerity does not make the evidence confirmatory: the development population and analysis family were reused. The tercile transition is left-to-right by construction, and its strictly upper triangle is exactly zero (0): in \(B[\text{next}, \text{current}]\) orientation a non-decreasing position puts mass on and below the diagonal. This project’s own first draft stated the invariant with the wrong triangle — decision 1’s orientation trap arriving in prose rather than in a matrix. The error surfaced only because the number was recorded rather than asserted (docs/decisions.md entry 26).

The directional recognition prediction and the prior-intervention anchors are recorded in decision 25. This development-session protocol does not establish independent confirmation: the development population was reused, and uncertainty must respect the document sampling unit.

4.9 Generation by expected-free-energy policy selection

Every level described so far is a recognition model: observations arrive and beliefs are updated. Generation is the other direction, and until this section it was apparatus without exercise — the expected free energy of eq. 2 was specified, C was zero at every level, and each level had a single trivial action, so there was nothing to select between.

That is not a missing feature so much as a half-specified model. A generative model that cannot generate has only been used in one direction.

4.9.1 Next-letter actions and policy selection

The generating agent is the letter level with a controllable transition. It has one action per symbol, and \(\mathbf{B}[\text{next}, \text{current}, k] = \delta(\text{next} = k)\): action \(k\) emits letter \(k\). Choosing an action is choosing the next symbol, which is what makes policy selection generation rather than an analogy.

Two quantities then compete. The policy prior \(\mathbf{E}\) is the learned Brown bigram column for the current letter — the agent’s habit, what it would do absent any goal. The preference vector \(\mathbf{C}\) is supplied top-down by the word level: given the prefix emitted so far, the lexicon posterior is supported on the vocabulary words carrying that prefix, and marginalizing it over each word’s next letter gives a distribution over what should come next. pymdp combines them as

\[q(\pi) \;=\; \sigma\!\left(\gamma\, \mathrm{neg\text{-}EFE} + \ln \mathbf{E}\right),\qquad{(13)}\]

with \(\gamma\) the policy precision that tbl. 17 sweeps.

This is the first place in AILM where one level sets another’s C, and the first non-flat C anywhere in the project. It is also the second inter-level channel attempted. The first ran from letters into phonemes and measured harmful (sec. 6.1); the reason was structural, that it carried strictly less information about the observed symbol than the observation itself. This channel is not in that position — it carries the lexicon, which the letter level does not possess in any form.

Under a controllable transition the corpus statistics change role rather than place. The bigram table is identical to Level 1’s; it is the policy prior here and the transition there, because the transition has become a structural consequence of the chosen action. A specification annotating it as the transition in this configuration would describe a model that cannot choose what to emit, which is why the generative agent carries its own GNN model rather than a flag on the recognition one.

4.9.2 Why membership cannot discriminate generation quality

The obvious measurement is the fraction of generated tokens that are real words. It is green by construction. The preference floors any letter that would leave the trie, so at any usable precision the generator essentially cannot emit a non-word: membership is 100% at the operating point, and also 100% at a precision where the model emits 1 distinct word forever.

A metric that cannot fail is not a gate, however good the number looks. Had membership been the gate, the degenerate generator would have passed it perfectly. This is the fourth occasion in this project on which the first metric anyone reaches for turned out to constrain nothing, and the pattern is now familiar enough to be worth stating as a rule: before adopting a metric, ask what configuration would fail it, and go and build that configuration.

The gate is instead the total-variation distance between the generated word distribution and the lexicon’s, against the exact word distribution induced by ancestral sampling from the letter bigram — the strongest generator with the same letter statistics and no top-down channel. Producing a real word is easy once the channel exists; producing the in the right proportion is the actual claim.

4.9.3 Generation controls and gate falsifiability

Three, and the first is an exact identity rather than a comparison. With \(\mathbf{C} = 0\) the policy posterior reduces to the habit, so the generator must reproduce ancestral sampling character-for-character under the same seed. Not approximately — the two are the same stochastic process, and the recorder refuses to write if they differ. That anchor is what licenses reading the whole sweep as an effect of the top-down channel rather than of anything else in the pipeline.

The anchor is paired with its own non-vacuity check, since a bug making the preference always zero would satisfy it while proving the opposite. And the third control replaces the preference with its letter axis reversed — a fixed involutive permutation, so it keeps its entropy and loses only its meaning. Membership falls to 0%. Replacing the preference with a uniform vector instead would have confounded content with entropy, which is why the reversal is the stronger control — the same argument that governs the inter-level coupling null.

Finally, the closed-form policy posterior that drives generation is checked against pymdp’s own infer_policies primitive: the historical fast generator never calls infer_policies itself, and the recorder measures the worst absolute deviation between the two posteriors over 120 (letter, prefix) states, refusing to write above its tolerance; the recorded value is 1.16e-07. An unproven fast path is a substitution rather than an optimization.

With the standalone generation mechanism characterized and its reduction measured, what remains is the question the stack has been deferring: whether anything passes between the levels. sec. 4.10 states the hypothesis and its test, and sec. 5 reports what each channel delivered.

4.10 Cross-level interventions and channel contracts

AILM is a stack of levels ordered by descriptive scale, and whether that stack is a hierarchy is the question this section measures rather than assumes. The vocabulary is kept separate throughout because the distinctions are separately checkable: a stack is levels arranged by scale, composition is one level’s alphabet or output structurally entering another’s, coupling is one level’s probability object actually changing another’s computation, and hierarchy is the stronger claim that cross-scale variables participate in a repeatedly interacting inferential architecture. AILM ships a stack with composition, and seven registered receiver interventions, five of them measured and the case-word bridge’s influence measured as an exploratory development-population sweep (sec. 5.10.4). It does not establish the fourth from those measurements. The connected development runtime described below is a separate engineering extension. By source kind, five have a model-output source and two have a privileged-oracle source. 6 levels are built, and the interventions have opposite outcomes: a letter-to-phoneme message that made the system significantly worse, an L3→L1g lexical preference that makes generation work, a lexicon-to-decoder channel that helps, an L6→L5 intervention on the receiver’s joint D prior, and a privileged punctuation-type-oracle→L3 word-prior intervention whose predicted harm did not reproduce (measured in sec. 5.10.3). The oracle arm does not use an L5 posterior. The last three are independently measured experiments, not stages in one cascade.

Connected development runtime. ailm.levels.connected.ConnectedRuntime executes the GNN-built levels on an explicit causal schedule. Document-position predictions set clause priors; clause predictions affect case priors; case beliefs set word priors before spelling arrives; and prefix-conditioned word beliefs change phone and letter predictions. Completed-token evidence updates the clause agent, and completed-sentence type beliefs update document position for subsequent sentences. Raw input contains normalized American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) lexical runs and sentence boundaries. Structured input may supply UPOS before spelling, but has no slot for case labels, dependency relations, morphology, phonemes or sentence-type labels. In raw-text mode, a fixed train-fitted lexical encoder supplies a soft UPOS observation after the current word has been processed. This encoder is retained in both connected and named-channel-disabled arms; because its input is the word belief, its outputs can differ between connected and named-channel-disabled execution. Bridge kernels are fitted from training inputs only. Each call resets document state, and the composition contract specifies the subordinate reset clocks. The resulting next-word prior can also drive bounded lexical continuation through live L1g infer_policies and sample_action calls.

This composition is a schedule of conditional updates, not an assertion of an exact posterior for a single global model. Local conditional reference checks, channel ablations, scrambled messages and reset controls exercise the mechanism; they do not by themselves establish a beneficial corpus-level effect. The separate, locally specified GUM comparison in sec. 5.1 evaluates the fixed schedule against disabling its named channels. Its channel strength is fixed before that evaluation rather than selected on its outcomes. The historical stage and channel measurements below are not reinterpreted as results for the connected runtime. The executable contract is docs/design/connected_runtime.md.

One of the two case-word seams carries a measured estimand as well. The L4→L3 case-word bridge’s influence sweep was registered before it ran (docs/decisions.md entry 121): the estimand is the per-token log-gain of the L3 word prior under the case-word inlet against the bit-identical zero-weight anchor, over the case-word artifact’s test documents, restricted to lowercase exact-string matches against the Stage 3 receiver vocabulary. The scored population is 3001 tokens across 64 documents, expanding to 14,449 word-level emissions under the whole-document clustered bootstrap; a token whose UPOS tag has no row in the case model’s observation alphabet stays in the stream under the no-message policy (D_α = D_0 exactly, 561 such tokens of 4 tags). The message is the model-sender marginalization of the case level’s own per-token role posterior; the privileged-oracle arm is a separately labeled diagnostic and remains unexecuted. The controls are the shipped ones: the bit-identical zero-weight anchor (the recorder records the bit-identity as 1 and the anchor’s non-vacuity as 1; 1 = verified), the scrambled-word negative control, and the declared positive control — the evaluation stream’s own pooled in-vocabulary unigram — which must lead the scrambled control by the pre-registered per-token margin of 0.177528463 nats at every positive weight; the recorder refuses without writing anything otherwise. The receiver arithmetic is the L3 word level’s own per-token scoring with the per-token UPOS observation in place of the clause type, and the sweep reuses the shipped mixing grid, mix_prior, and clustered summaries unchanged. Scope, stated as the registration states it: development evidence under a fresh registration, never confirmatory — the scored documents are the already-scored EWT dev population in a new representation — with cross-corpus transfer (an EWT-estimated message applied to the Stage 3 Brown-receiver vocabulary) part of the estimand and named as such, and the recorded receiver sensitivities of the other arms describing their own interventions and bounding nothing here.

Results with opposite signs are an anecdote unless something explains them all. This section states the explanation, derives a prediction from it, and reports a test of that prediction that was specified before it ran.

4.10.1 Information-value hypothesis for cross-level messages

Working hypothesis (information value). This hypothesis separates what a message could deliver from what it actually delivers, holding the receiver and the loss function fixed. Fix the receiving level and score it under a proper predictive loss (Gneiting and Raftery 2007) — a loss that a forecaster minimizes exactly by reporting its true beliefs. Under that setup, an inter-level message has positive potential value to the extent that it carries conditional information about the receiver’s target beyond what the receiver already has. Under logarithmic loss, that potential value equals exactly \(I(Y; M \mid X)\) — the conditional mutual information between the target \(Y\) and the message \(M\), given what the receiver already observes, \(X\) — but only for a Bayes-optimal receiver, one whose belief update is exact (Jiao et al. 2015). Realized value is different: it is a property of the receiving side rather than of the sender. It depends on how the receiver is misspecified, on how well the message is calibrated, on where and by what rule the message is inserted, and on how sensitive the receiver’s likelihood is to the latent variable the message moves.

Realized value is not bounded above by potential value when the receiver is misspecified, and AILM’s receivers are finite and misspecified by construction. Write \(q_0\) for the receiver before the message and \(q_1\) for the receiver after it. eq. 14 decomposes the log-loss reduction into three terms:

\[\Delta_{\log} = I(Y; M \mid X) + \mathbb{E}_X\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p(Y \mid X) \,\|\, q_0(Y \mid X)\right) - \mathbb{E}_{X,M}\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p(Y \mid X, M) \,\|\, q_1(Y \mid X, M)\right).\qquad{(14)}\]

The first term is the conditional mutual information above; the second and third measure how far the receiver’s beliefs sit from the truth before and after the message arrives. Because of these extra terms, a message that moves a badly misspecified receiver toward the correct distribution can deliver more than its conditional mutual information alone would predict. Conversely, a poorly inserted message can destroy performance even while that information is strictly positive. All three terms are separately measurable, which makes the empirical program sharper rather than weaker: source information, receiver sensitivity, and mismatch correction are three distinct mechanisms, and the channels below are read against all three.

The coupling sweep and its harm were already known when the hypothesis was formulated. The lexical sweep’s sign and interior optimum shape were then registered before that sweep ran, and the sign held while the shape did not survive the correction of decision 110; the earlier coupling shape supplied the motivating contrast, not an independent prospective confirmation. The hypothesis’s support is its measured channels, not a proof of universality.

Novelty — conditional information the receiver lacks — is the first term. The lexical and clause-channel predictions were prospectively specified against that term (decision 27 in a prior commit; decisions 18–19 within one development session); the earlier coupling result was already in hand and motivated the criterion.

The hypothesis is deliberately not a biconditional. “A message helps exactly when it is novel to the receiver” is the sharper statement, and it fails in both directions under the machinery this paper actually runs. One of the two failures is measured inside this section.

Novel and still harmful. Messages here enter by linear mixing at a weight, and linear mixing is not the combination rule a correctly structured receiver would use. Novelty is a property of the message; the weight is not. The lexical channel was the demonstration of this until its backoff was corrected (decision 110). Under the defective lookup, the same message into the same receiver helped at one weight and cost accuracy at the highest. Under the documented rule, it helps at every tested weight instead: by 3.333 points at weight 0.7, and by 3.258 at weight 0.9. The structural point survives the correction even though its example did not: conditional information is identical at every weight, so a weight-dependent sign, where one occurs, cannot come from the message’s content. Finite-sample estimation is a second route to the same outcome. The message is a statistic estimated on a training split, so what is delivered on a held-out item can point the wrong way even when the underlying quantity is informative.

Redundant and still helpful. A receiver whose own model is misspecified can be moved in the right direction by a message that would add nothing to a correctly specified predictor, because the message redistributes mass the receiver had mis-assigned. That is regularization rather than information, and it is indistinguishable from information if the only instrument is the sign of an end-to-end effect. The punctuation-type-oracle→word-prior intervention of sec. 5.10.3 is the measured case this paper cannot rule that reading out on.

Both failure modes are about the receiver and the delivery, which is why the hypothesis separates potential value from realized value rather than hedging the biconditional.

The hypothesis accounts for the existing results structurally, without appeal to their magnitudes.

The letter-to-phoneme channel carries no potential value because at position \(t\) the letter-to-phone level already observes letter \(t\), while the letter level’s predictive is a function of letters \(0 \ldots t-1\). The message is a strictly weaker statement about the very symbol the receiver can see, so mixing it in substitutes weak evidence for a certainty. Accuracy fell monotonically in the mixing weight, which is what a message with nothing to add looks like: there is no weight at which saying it more loudly helps.

The lexicon-to-letter channel carries potential value because a bigram cannot represent “only these letter sequences are words” at any order below the length of the longest word. The lexicon is information the letter level does not possess in any form.

4.10.2 Prospective lexical-sweep prediction

A hypothesis that only ever explains results already in hand explains nothing. The test holds the receiving level fixed and changes the sender: a lexical message into the same letter-to-phone level the first channel harmed.

It does not hold everything else fixed, and the claim of control is exactly this narrow. The two messages enter the receiver at different places — the letter predictive folds into the observation likelihood over phones, the lexical message mixes into the phone predictive — so message source is not the only variable that differs between the sweeps. The factorial version of this experiment crosses letter versus lexical source with evidence versus predictive insertion, holding receiver, mixing rule, weight grid, and evaluation positions fixed across every combination. The sweeps below occupy the letter-at-evidence and lexicon-at-predictive combinations; the crossed combinations are reported in sec. 11, which is where the attribution this paragraph could not make is made.

The message is \(p(\text{phone}_t \mid \text{letter prefix } 0 \ldots t)\), estimated on the training split and applied to held-out pairs, mixed linearly into the phone predictive. It is conditioned on the prefix rather than on word identity for a reason that sec. 4.6 makes concrete: the lexicon maps word to pronunciation, so conditioning on identity would turn the task into a dictionary lookup and any improvement would be circular. A prefix statistic evaluated on held-out words can be wrong, which is the property that makes it a measurement.

The prediction recorded before the experiment was that the channel would help, and would do so non-monotonically — an interior optimum being the signature the hypothesis expected from a message the receiver lacks.

4.10.3 Fixed and varying factors in channel comparisons

This table lines up the measured channels side by side so the one variable they do not hold fixed — where the message enters the receiver — is visible rather than buried in the numbers.

Letter → phoneme Lexicon → phoneme
Message letter predictive over \(0 \ldots t-1\) lexical prefix statistic
Novel to the receiver? no — the level observes letter \(t\) yes — the level has no lexicon
Enters the receiver at the observation likelihood over phones the phone predictive
Shape in the mixing weight monotone decline rise to a plateau (interior argmax, not distinguished from the top weight)
Sign at the best recorded weight -0.2639 points at weight 0.1 +3.333 points at weight 0.7

Both figures in the last row are recorded at the weight that scored best on the grid, so they are read the same way; for the coupling that is the least harmful weight, because the decline is monotone and every larger weight costs more. Direction and receiving level are matched, and both messages are linear mixtures whose zero-weight end is the uncoupled decode exactly. Rows two and three of the table are the two variables that differ together: the pair varies novelty and insertion point at once, so it cannot attribute the opposite signs to either alone. The coupling result was already known; it motivated the potential-value account and the later registered lexical prediction. The lexical result supports that prediction, while an insertion-point account of the two signs remains available.

4.10.4 Registered proper-loss estimand

Every channel number above is an argmax accuracy. The working-hypothesis box at the head of this section is not stated on that axis: it is stated under a proper predictive loss (Gneiting and Raftery 2007), and accuracy is not one. Accuracy is a threshold statistic on the receiver’s posterior, so a perturbation that moves mass without moving the argmax is invisible to it, and one that flips a few near-ties can move it in either direction while the receiver’s actual belief about the target gets worse. The two axes can therefore disagree in both sign and shape, and until they have been put side by side on the same positions, a monotone decline over the whole grid is a property of the statistic as much as of the channel. For the letter-at-evidence cell of the channel factorial the two axes have since been put side by side on the same positions (sec. 11): they agree in sign and in shape class, so for that cell the decline is a property of the channel.

4.11 Verification by Mutation Controls and Independent Decoder Agreement

The verification apparatus is not scaffolding around the result — it is a deliverable of the same standing as the levels themselves. Both defects that reached a shipped state in this project (sec. 4.3, sec. 4.4) were invisible to every structural check available: pymdp validated the matrices, the suite was green, and the reported numbers cleared the declared thresholds. What surfaced them was a control that could fail and an instrument that did not share code with the thing it measured. This section describes those two mechanisms. It describes the decoder-equivalence result that lets a closed-form oracle stand in for pymdp on full-corpus statistics, and the statistical procedures the paired claims are judged by and what each of them assumes. It describes the two design facts — clustered sampling units and a retrospectively assembled test family — that bound what any of those procedures can be read to establish, the convention under which an interval-spanning result is reported as a bound rather than as an absence, and the ledger that binds every number in this manuscript to a recorded run. Both bounding facts are stated here, before sec. 5 reports the numbers they qualify, because a caveat that arrives after the claim it conditions has already been read as unconditional. Each mechanism is stated with the failure it forecloses and, where one exists, the failure it does not: a verification layer described only by what it checks is indistinguishable from one that checks nothing.

4.11.1 Positive controls and required mutation failures

Every gate carries a positive and a negative control.

src/ailm/control.py defines ControlHarness and GateVacuousError, and it offers two services that are easy to conflate and do different work. The first, assert_gate_is_live(good_value, bad_value, direction), compares a good model against a deliberately degraded one directly, using the degraded score as the bar. It raises GateVacuousError when the two scores are identical — a metric that returns the same number for a working and a broken model is measuring nothing — and it fails an assertion when the good model is merely not better. It says nothing at all about where the declared threshold sits. The second, verify_negative_control_fails(metric_fn, broken_input, threshold, direction), is the one the threshold enters: it re-runs the metric function on broken input and raises GateVacuousError if the broken result strictly passes the bar. Both inherit the strict comparison of gate_passes in src/ailm/gates.py (eq. 10), so a broken model landing exactly on the bar is treated as having failed it. The boundary is resolved against the gate rather than against the model, which is the conservative direction for a vacuity check.

The distinction that makes this worth the machinery: a passing positive control establishes only that the number is achievable. A failing negative control establishes that the gate detects that planted defect under the tested conditions; it does not establish that every faulty model fails. A threshold no broken model can fail, or no working model can pass, is not a weak test, it is not a test — and the two defects in sec. 10.1 are both instances of exactly that, reached from opposite directions.

What the harness does not do is worth stating with equal precision, because a control that is trusted beyond its scope is the next defect.
